Local sensitivity: perturb the input slightly (change one benign word in a log entry) and measure how much the explanation changes; a faithful explanation should change only proportionally to the input change; large explanation changes for small input changes indicate instability. Inter-method consistency: compute rank correlation between LIME and SHAP importance rankings on the same input; high inter-method consistency (>0.7) provides evidence that multiple methods are capturing the same underlying model behavior; low consistency warrants caution about trusting either explanation in isolation. (3) Human utility metrics -- Task completion accuracy: present analysts with security classification tasks with and without AI explanations; measure whether explanations improve analyst classification accuracy; for alert triage, compare analyst true positive rate and false positive rate with explanation support vs. score-only; a utility-positive explanation should improve analyst accuracy by a measurable amount. Time to decision: measure analyst decision time with and without explanations; high-quality explanations should reduce decision time for clear-cut cases (the explanation immediately confirms or refutes the threat); for ambiguous cases, explanations may increase decision time as analysts engage more deeply, which can be acceptable if it leads to better decisions. Trust calibration quality: compare analyst confidence in their decisions to actual decision accuracy with and without explanations; well-calibrated trust (analyst confidence matches actual accuracy) indicates that explanations are helping analysts correctly calibrate their reliance on the AI; overconfidence (high analyst confidence despite errors) indicates the explanation is misleading. (4) Security-specific evaluation metrics -- ATT&CK alignment: for security LLM explanations, measure the proportion of explanations that correctly identify relevant ATT&CK techniques; evaluate by comparing model-identified techniques against analyst-labeled ground truth for the same alerts; high ATT&CK alignment confirms that explanations are grounded in the correct security concepts. IOC specificity: measure whether explanations cite specific IOCs (concrete IP addresses, domain names, file hashes) that are actually present in the input vs. generic descriptions; high IOC specificity confirms the explanation is grounded in the actual evidence rather than generic security language. False positive prediction: measure whether explanation quality metrics (coherence, specificity, ATT&CK alignment) predict false positives; run logistic regression with explanation quality features as predictors and false positive label as outcome; a significant model confirms that explanation quality is a useful proxy for detection quality, enabling explanation-quality-based triage prioritization. (5) Operational impact metrics -- Alert fatigue reduction: measure the reduction in alert volume that human analysts must manually review after deploying explanation-based triage (routing high-quality explanations to automated processing and low-quality explanations to human review); a high-quality explanation system should reduce manual review volume by 30-50% while maintaining or improving true positive rate. Mean time to escalation: measure the time from alert generation to escalation decision for alerts processed with explanation support vs. without; explanation support should reduce mean time to escalation for straightforward alerts while maintaining thoroughness for ambiguous ones. Analyst satisfaction: measure analyst satisfaction with explanation quality using structured surveys (explanation relevance, explanation clarity, explanation actionability each rated 1-5); benchmark explanation satisfaction against best-in-class commercial security tools to assess relative quality; analyst satisfaction directly predicts adoption -- a technically excellent explanation system that analysts find confusing or irrelevant will not improve security outcomes.

instruction: How do natural language explanations generated by LLMs differ from numerical attribution explanations, and when is each more appropriate in security contexts?
output: LLMs can produce two fundamentally different types of explanations: numerical attributions (SHAP values, LIME weights, attention scores) that quantify feature importance, and natural language explanations that express reasoning in human-readable text. Each has distinct strengths and weaknesses that determine their appropriateness for different security contexts. NL vs. numerical explanations: (1) Numerical attribution explanations -- Characteristics: produce a score or weight for each input feature quantifying its importance to the prediction; examples: SHAP values (signed, additive, theoretically grounded); LIME weights (linear surrogate coefficients); attention weights (raw attention probabilities); gradient-based scores (integrated gradients, gradient times input). Strengths: mathematical precision (the score for a token is a specific number that can be compared, ranked, and thresholded); reproducibility (the same method on the same input produces the same scores, modulo random sampling variance); systematic evaluation (faithfulness, stability, and cross-method consistency can be measured using defined metrics); integration with downstream systems (numerical attributions can be parsed, filtered, and aggregated programmatically). Limitations: requires interpretation (a SHAP value of +0.43 is meaningless without domain context -- the analyst must know that +0.43 is high for this feature type and what direction is positive); expert user requirement (non-expert analysts may struggle to interpret SHAP values or integrate them into triage decisions); no reasoning chain (numerical attributions show what was important but not why it is important in the security context). (2) Natural language explanations -- Characteristics: the model generates a text description of its reasoning, e.g.: this PowerShell command is classified as malicious because it uses Base64 encoding to hide its payload (-EncodedCommand), downloads and executes code from a remote server using Invoke-Expression, and the network destination uses a non-standard port consistent with attacker-controlled infrastructure. These indicators match the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001 (PowerShell) with obfuscation (T1027). Strengths: directly understandable (analysts read explanations in their professional language without additional interpretation skill); reasoning chain (natural language captures the causal chain -- not just what was important, but why it matters); alignment with analyst mental models (experienced analysts think in terms of TTPs, kill chain stages, and threat actor patterns -- natural language explanations that use this vocabulary align with analyst cognition); flexible detail level (the explanation can be brief for simple cases and detailed for complex ones). Limitations: faithfulness uncertainty (natural language explanations generated by LLMs may not faithfully represent internal model computations -- the model may confabulate a plausible explanation that does not match its actual reasoning process); evaluation difficulty (natural language explanation quality is harder to measure than numerical attribution faithfulness); systematic analysis difficulty (natural language explanations cannot be directly aggregated or statistically analyzed without additional NLP processing). (3) When to use numerical attributions in security -- Automated processing pipelines: SHAP values can be parsed programmatically to extract top features, validate ATT&CK alignment, and compute explanation quality metrics; automated triage routing based on numerical attribution quality requires machine-readable scores. Model evaluation and validation: technical evaluation of explanation faithfulness, stability, and consistency requires numerical attributions; natural language explanations cannot be input to comprehensiveness or AOPC computation. Red team and model development: security researchers analyzing model weaknesses, bias, or shortcut learning require precise numerical attributions that can be aggregated and statistically analyzed across many examples. Expert analyst research: threat hunters and detection engineers who need to understand model behavior at a technical level benefit from numerical attributions that reveal the precise features driving detections. (4) When to use natural language explanations in security -- First-tier analyst triage: analysts performing initial alert review need quick, interpretable explanations; natural language explanations provide immediate context without requiring interpretation of numerical scores. Analyst training: natural language explanations of model decisions serve as training material for junior analysts, conveying security reasoning in an accessible format. Threat intelligence reporting: natural language explanations of AI-detected threats can be incorporated directly into threat reports and incident documentation. Executive and non-technical stakeholder communication: natural language summaries of AI security decisions are suitable for board-level briefings and regulatory reports where numerical attributions would be inappropriate. Orion-XAI deployment: Orion-XAI is designed to generate natural language explanations by default, as the Alpaca training format teaches explanation through natural language output; the hallucination risk score provides quantitative confidence assessment alongside natural language reasoning. (5) Hybrid approaches for security -- Best-practice security LLM deployments combine both: natural language explanation as the default output for analyst consumption, generated by the LLM as part of its standard output format; numerical attribution (SHAP) computed asynchronously and available as expandable detail for analysts who want technical evidence; automated quality metrics computed from numerical attributions to validate natural language explanation quality before presenting to analysts; and feedback loop where numerical attribution analysis identifies systematic explanation failures that are corrected by fine-tuning the natural language explanation generation.

instruction: How can XAI methods explain LLM decisions in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) processing, including entity extraction and relationship inference?
output: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) processing involves extracting structured information (entities, relationships, TTPs) from unstructured threat reports. LLMs are increasingly used for automated CTI processing; explanation methods enable analysts to validate extraction quality and understand model reasoning. XAI for CTI LLMs: (1) CTI processing tasks and explanation requirements -- Named entity recognition (NER) for CTI: identifying threat actors, malware families, CVEs, IPs, domains, attack tools, and targeted sectors from threat report text; explanation need: which tokens in the source text were used to identify each entity -- a threat actor identified with high support (multiple mentions in diverse contexts) is more reliable than one identified from a single ambiguous mention. Relationship extraction: identifying relationships between CTI entities (APT28 uses Mimikatz; CVE-2021-44228 affects Apache Log4j; Lazarus Group targets cryptocurrency exchanges); explanation need: what textual evidence supports each extracted relationship -- a relationship supported by an explicit sentence in the source text (APT28 was observed using Mimikatz) is more reliable than one inferred from proximity of entity mentions. TTP mapping: classifying described behaviors as MITRE ATT&CK techniques; explanation need: which specific sentences or phrases in the source text support the ATT&CK classification -- a TTP mapped with direct textual evidence is more reliable than one inferred from general context. (2) SHAP for CTI entity extraction explanation -- Token-level attribution for entity extraction: for each extracted entity mention, SHAP attributions show which surrounding tokens provided the most evidence for the entity classification; threat actor extraction (for text identified as containing a threat actor mention, SHAP highlights: the threat actor name itself, associated technical terms used in conjunction -- malware names, CVE references, targeted industry terms -- and TTPs mentioned in the sentence; high-confidence entity extraction shows SHAP values concentrated on the entity name and its technical context); CVE extraction (SHAP attribution for CVE identification highlights: the CVE ID format tokens, product names in proximity, and terms like vulnerability, exploit, patch -- confirming the model identifies CVEs based on the correct lexical and semantic pattern rather than spurious correlations). Negative SHAP values for entity extraction: tokens with negative SHAP values push against the entity classification; in ambiguous text, negative-importance tokens help analysts understand what features distinguish a legitimate entity mention from a false positive extraction. (3) Attention and SHAP for relationship inference -- Relationship evidence visualization: for an extracted relationship (APT28 -- uses -- Mimikatz), attention and SHAP can show which sentence fragment provides the core evidence; span-level attribution: aggregate SHAP values at the span level (a sentence or clause) rather than the token level; the span with highest aggregate SHAP provides the key evidence sentence for the relationship; analysts can verify the evidence sentence exists in the source text and accurately describes the relationship. Cross-sentence relationship inference: some relationships are inferable only from multiple sentences in combination; for multi-sentence inferences, attention patterns show the model attending to relevant mentions across a long document; SHAP with sentence-level aggregation identifies which sentences jointly support the inferred relationship -- this enables analysts to evaluate whether the inference is well-supported by multiple independent evidence points or depends on a single ambiguous statement. (4) Explanation-based CTI quality assessment -- CTI extraction confidence scoring: combine SHAP attribution strength, span-level evidence support, and entity recognition consistency into a per-extraction confidence score; high-confidence extractions (strong SHAP attribution, explicit evidence span, consistent across document) are suitable for automated STIX bundle population; low-confidence extractions (weak attribution, implicit evidence, inconsistent with other document context) are queued for human analyst validation before CTI dissemination. Source credibility integration: explanation methods can integrate source credibility into confidence scoring; an entity extracted with high SHAP support from a sentence that cites a primary source (observed in network traffic vs. reportedly used) receives higher confidence than the same entity extracted from a hearsay or secondary source. (5) Explainable CTI pipeline architecture -- End-to-end explainable CTI pipeline: ingestion (threat report ingested from OSINT feeds, commercial TI platforms, ISAC sharing); LLM extraction (Orion-XAI processes the report for entity and relationship extraction with structured explanation output); SHAP attribution (computed asynchronously for each extraction); confidence scoring (per-extraction confidence combining SHAP and NLI entailment); analyst review queue (low-confidence extractions with their evidence spans presented to CTI analysts for validation); STIX population (validated and high-confidence extractions automatically populate STIX bundles for sharing via TAXII); ATT&CK enrichment (TTP extractions validated and mapped to ATT&CK technique IDs using explanation-validated evidence). Audit trail: every extraction in the STIX bundle is tagged with its source evidence span and confidence score; downstream consumers can assess extraction quality; CTI sharing platforms can filter by minimum confidence threshold, ensuring that shared CTI meets recipient quality standards.

instruction: How should a security LLM fine-tuning dataset be designed to produce models with strong explainability capabilities?
output: Designing a fine-tuning dataset for a security LLM that produces strong explainability requires deliberate dataset engineering -- the model will learn to explain in the style and at the quality level of its training data. If training examples contain vague, post-hoc, or inaccurate explanations, the fine-tuned model will produce the same. Designing security LLM datasets for explainability: (1) Explanation quality principles for training data -- Specificity principle: training explanations must cite specific evidence from the input, not generic security observations; poor example: this is suspicious because it shows unusual behavior; good example: this is suspicious because the process spawns cmd.exe immediately after reading from a registry Run key -- a persistence-followed-by-execution pattern consistent with T1547.001 and T1059.003. Evidence grounding: each claim in the training explanation should be traceable to a specific element of the input; for log analysis training examples, each point in the explanation should cite a specific log entry or event; unexplained or unsupported claims in training data teach the model to confabulate. ATT&CK alignment: training explanations for security classification should include explicit ATT&CK technique references where applicable; models trained on ATT&CK-aligned explanations learn to produce ATT&CK-structured outputs, directly improving operational utility for SOC analysts. (2) Structured explanation format in training data -- Consistent output structure: training examples should use a consistent explanation format that the model learns to reproduce; recommended format elements: Classification (Malicious/Anomalous/Benign with confidence level), Key indicators (specific evidence elements numbered for clarity), Reasoning chain (explicit step-by-step reasoning connecting evidence to conclusion), ATT&CK mapping (technique IDs for each indicator), Confidence basis (what would increase or decrease confidence), and Recommended action (initial triage or investigation step). Format consistency: use exactly the same format across all training examples of the same type; inconsistent formats produce models that generate inconsistently structured outputs, making downstream parsing difficult; if SOC integration requires machine-readable outputs, the training format should match the required schema. CoT integration: training examples should include chain-of-thought reasoning (explicit intermediate reasoning steps) rather than direct classification with explanation; CoT training improves both explanation quality and classification accuracy. (3) Diversity requirements for explainability training data -- Coverage across threat categories: training data should include explainable examples across all major security domains (network, endpoint, identity, cloud, application) and threat categories (malware, phishing, intrusion, data exfiltration, insider threat); coverage gaps produce a model that generates poor explanations for underrepresented threat types. Diversity in input formats: train on explanations for multiple input types (structured logs, unstructured threat reports, alerts from different security tools, network flow data); diverse input training produces a model that generalizes explanation format across input types rather than overfitting to a specific format. Diversity in explanation styles: include explanations at multiple detail levels (brief summary explanations and detailed deep-dive explanations) and from multiple analyst perspectives (tier-1 triage perspective and threat hunter research perspective); this enables the model to adapt explanation depth to context. (4) Negative examples in explainability training -- Explicit uncertainty training: include training examples where the correct response is to express uncertainty rather than a confident classification; these examples should model the reasoning for uncertainty (this log sequence has two plausible interpretations -- legitimate administrative activity or lateral movement; the following additional context would distinguish them: ...); training on explicit uncertainty responses reduces model overconfidence. Correction examples: include training examples showing an initial misclassification followed by a correction upon seeing additional context; these examples teach the model to update its explanation when new evidence is introduced, important for multi-turn security investigations. False positive explanation training: include labeled false positive examples with explanations of why the detection was incorrect; models trained to understand false positive patterns can generate explanations that explicitly flag features commonly associated with false positives, improving analyst triage efficiency. (5) Quality assurance for explainability training data -- Expert review: all explanation training examples should be reviewed by security domain experts before inclusion; automated quality checks (ATT&CK technique ID validation, specificity scoring via information density metrics) can pre-filter low-quality explanations before expert review. Adversarial example review: test candidate training examples by generating model outputs for the same inputs before and after training; if post-training outputs are worse than pre-training outputs on specific inputs, those training examples may be contaminated or incorrect; investigate and remove problematic examples. Hallucination contamination check: audit training examples for hallucinated content (CVE numbers that do not exist, threat actor attributions that are fabricated); hallucinated training data teaches the model to hallucinate with confidence; use automated CVE, ATT&CK technique, and threat actor name verification against authoritative sources as part of the training data quality pipeline. Orion-XAI dataset design: the xai_cybersec_additions.jsonl dataset applies these principles -- each training example follows the instruction-output Alpaca format with structured, specific, ATT&CK-aligned explanations; the 3000-example target provides sufficient coverage across security domains for a 3B parameter model with LoRA fine-tuning.

instruction: What are the key considerations for deploying explainable AI in high-stakes security decisions such as incident escalation and breach notification?
output: High-stakes security decisions -- incident escalation to executive leadership, breach notification to regulators and affected individuals, attribution claims shared with law enforcement -- carry significant legal, financial, and reputational consequences. Deploying AI explanation methods in these contexts requires heightened standards for reliability, auditability, and human oversight. XAI for high-stakes security decisions: (1) Why high-stakes decisions require stronger XAI standards -- Consequence magnitude: a wrongly confirmed breach notification triggers regulatory fines (GDPR up to 4% of global annual turnover, HIPAA up to $1.9M per violation), customer notification costs, and reputational damage; a missed escalation allows threat actors additional dwell time; these consequences demand higher AI reliability and explanation quality than routine alert triage. Accountability requirements: high-stakes decisions require accountable decision-making -- a human decision-maker must be identifiable for each consequential decision; AI-assisted decisions are acceptable only if a human reviewed and endorsed the AI recommendation; the explanation must be sufficient for the human reviewer to make an independent judgment, not merely ratify the AI output. Legal and regulatory scrutiny: breach notifications may be subject to discovery in litigation; AI-assisted decisions may be challenged in court or regulatory proceedings; explanation audit trails must be comprehensive, accurate, and defensible under legal scrutiny. (2) Explanation standards for incident escalation -- Minimum explanation quality for escalation: incident escalation explanations should meet a higher quality bar than routine triage explanations; required elements: primary evidence (specific, source-attributed indicators supporting the escalation); temporal analysis (timeline of events from initial indicator to current state); scope assessment (estimated systems, data, and business functions affected); attribution assessment (any evidence linking the incident to known threat actors, with confidence and evidence basis explicitly stated); alternative hypotheses (alternative explanations for the observed indicators and why they are less probable). Explanation audit trail: the explanation used for each escalation decision must be archived with: model version, explanation method, human reviewer identity and timestamp, and whether the reviewer accepted, modified, or overrode the AI recommendation; this audit trail supports both post-incident review and regulatory compliance. Independent validation: for board-level escalations, require independent validation of the AI explanation by a second senior security professional; the validator reviews the explanation against the raw evidence independently -- not just endorsing the AI output but independently assessing the evidence. (3) Explanation standards for breach notification -- Regulatory requirements: GDPR Article 33 requires notification to supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach; HIPAA Breach Notification Rule requires notification within 60 days; SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules require material incident disclosure within 4 business days. AI explanation role in breach determination: AI assistance can accelerate breach determination by processing large log volumes rapidly; however, the breach determination itself must be endorsed by a qualified human decision-maker (CISO or legal counsel); the AI explanation provides the evidence basis for this determination but does not constitute the determination itself. Explanation completeness for breach notification: breach notification explanations must document: evidence that unauthorized access occurred (with source-attributed indicators); evidence of data scope (which data categories were exposed, with log evidence); timeline (when the breach began, when it was discovered, estimated duration); and evidence that the breach has been contained (or why it cannot be confirmed as contained). (4) Auditability and reproducibility requirements -- Explanation reproducibility: the explanation produced for a high-stakes decision must be reproducible -- running the same explanation method on the same input at a later time must produce the same result; this requires pinning model version, explanation method parameters, and random seeds; for stochastic methods (LIME, MC Dropout), log the random seed used and verify reproducibility before archiving. Version control for AI decisions: every AI-assisted high-stakes decision must record: model name and version (orion-xai-v2, specific adapter hash), explanation method and version, input data timestamp and hash (to verify the explanation corresponds to the actual data), and output explanation with timestamp. Immutable audit log: archive AI decision audit trails in an immutable log (append-only database or blockchain-anchored hash) to prevent retrospective modification; in legal proceedings, immutable logs provide evidence integrity that mutable records cannot. (5) Human oversight processes for high-stakes AI-assisted decisions -- Decision authority matrix: define which decisions can be AI-assisted (routine escalation triage), which require AI plus single human review (escalation to CISO), and which require AI plus multiple independent reviewers (board-level escalation, breach notification, law enforcement reporting); the decision authority matrix formalizes AI roles and human oversight requirements. Override and challenge process: any reviewer should be able to flag concerns with an AI explanation; a concern-flagging process should trigger: review of the specific concern by a qualified second reviewer; if concern is validated, escalation to senior decision-maker; documentation of the concern, review outcome, and final decision rationale. AI refusal escalation: for high-stakes decision support, configure the AI to refuse to provide a definitive recommendation when explanation quality is below threshold; instead, the AI presents the evidence and explicitly states that the evidence is insufficient for a high-confidence recommendation, requesting human judgment; this prevents AI overconfidence from becoming a liability in high-stakes decisions.

instruction: How does gradient-based saliency mapping explain LLM decisions in network intrusion detection?
output: Gradient-based saliency maps compute the gradient of the model output with respect to the input embedding, revealing which input tokens have the largest influence on the prediction. Unlike SHAP or LIME which rely on perturbations, saliency maps use a single forward and backward pass, making them computationally efficient for real-time security applications. Gradient saliency for network intrusion detection: (1) Computing saliency for network log LLMs -- Saliency computation: for a model f(x) producing classification logit y_c for class c, the saliency map is: S_i = |dy_c / dx_i|, the absolute gradient of the class logit with respect to each input embedding dimension; aggregate across the embedding dimension (L1 or L2 norm) to get a scalar saliency score per token. Efficient computation: a single backward pass through the model computes saliency for all input tokens simultaneously; for a 3B parameter model, this takes approximately the same time as a forward pass (milliseconds), making saliency computationally feasible for real-time alert explanation. For network intrusion detection: input is a sequence of tokenized network log entries (source IP, destination IP, port, protocol, bytes, flags, timestamp); saliency scores identify which specific log tokens drive the anomaly classification. (2) Saliency interpretation for intrusion detection -- Port scan detection: given a log sequence classified as a port scan, saliency scores highlight: repeated connections to multiple destination ports (high saliency on destination port tokens with high variance); short connection durations (high saliency on duration/byte count tokens near zero); single source IP with many destinations or many ports (high saliency on source IP token when it appears repeatedly across many connections). The saliency map translates to a plain-language explanation: the classification is primarily driven by the pattern of connections from source IP 192.168.1.45 to 253 distinct destination ports within 60 seconds, with connection durations consistently below 100ms -- consistent with a SYN scan pattern (T1046 Network Service Discovery). Data exfiltration detection: high saliency on outbound byte count tokens significantly exceeding the 30-day baseline for that source-destination pair; high saliency on destination IP tokens matching geolocation anomalies; the saliency explanation cites the specific transfer size and destination as the primary evidence. (3) Saliency vs. gradient-times-input -- Raw gradient saliency limitation: gradients measure the local rate of change of the output with respect to the input; they do not account for the magnitude of the input value itself; a token may have a high gradient but low actual value (or vice versa), so the raw gradient may not accurately reflect the token's actual importance. Gradient-times-input: element-wise product of the gradient and the input embedding; this combines rate-of-change sensitivity with actual input magnitude; for network intrusion detection: a large outbound byte count token with a high gradient produces a high gradient-times-input score -- correctly identifying that a large transfer is important; a rarely-occurring port number token with a high gradient also scores high -- correctly identifying that unusual port usage is important. Integrated Gradients superiority: IG addresses the saturation problem (the gradient may be near zero at the actual input even for important features because the model is in a saturated activation region); IG integrates along the path from baseline to input, capturing importance even when the gradient at the final input is small; for network intrusion detection, IG generally outperforms raw gradient saliency on faithfulness metrics. (4) Real-time saliency for SOC integration -- Latency requirements: SOC alert processing may have sub-second latency requirements; gradient saliency is fast enough (one forward + backward pass); SHAP KernelExplainer is too slow for real-time (requires hundreds of model evaluations); deploy gradient saliency for real-time explanation and SHAP for asynchronous deep-dive explanation on escalated alerts. Streaming saliency architecture: for high-volume network log processing, run the classifier and gradient saliency computation in a single GPU batch; return the alert classification and saliency map together; the saliency computation adds less than 10% overhead to the classification computation. Saliency visualization in the SOC dashboard: display network log entries in a table with token-level highlighting proportional to saliency score; high-saliency tokens appear in red; the visualization provides immediate visual explanation of which log entries drove the detection without requiring analysts to interpret numerical scores. (5) Limitations and mitigations for network intrusion saliency -- Gradient saturation: in deep models, gradients may saturate (approach zero) for correctly classified inputs; the model is confident and locally insensitive to small changes, so gradients are small even though the features are genuinely important; mitigation: use Integrated Gradients or SmoothGrad (average gradients over inputs with added Gaussian noise) to reduce saturation artifacts. Adversarial gradient manipulation: a sophisticated attacker who knows the saliency explanation system is being used could craft network traffic that manipulates gradient saliency to highlight benign-looking tokens while the actual malicious traffic hides in low-saliency positions; monitor for anomalies in the saliency distribution itself (unusually uniform saliency scores may indicate adversarial manipulation of the explanation system). Input preprocessing effects: network log tokenization choices affect saliency interpretation; tokenizing IP addresses as single tokens versus character-level tokens changes the granularity of saliency; ensure tokenization choices align with the desired explanation granularity.

instruction: How do LLM-based security systems handle multi-modal inputs such as network traffic combined with endpoint telemetry, and how are cross-modal explanations generated?
output: Modern enterprise security environments generate multiple telemetry streams simultaneously -- network traffic, endpoint process activity, identity/authentication logs, and cloud API calls. LLM-based security systems that fuse these streams require explanation methods that can attribute decisions across modalities. Multi-modal security LLM explanation: (1) Multi-modal security input architectures -- Early fusion: all modalities are combined before LLM processing; network log tokens, endpoint event tokens, and authentication log tokens are concatenated into a single input sequence; the LLM processes the combined sequence, and standard explanation methods (SHAP, attention) operate on the full multi-modal token sequence; advantage: the model can learn cross-modal interactions directly; challenge: the combined sequence may exceed context limits for long observation windows. Late fusion: each modality is processed by a separate encoder; the per-modality representations are combined (concatenated, averaged, or processed by a cross-modal attention layer) before final classification; advantage: each modality encoder can be optimized for its input type; challenge: explanations must span both per-modality explanations and cross-modal interaction explanations. Cross-attention fusion: specialized cross-attention layers allow one modality representation to attend to another; network representations attend to relevant endpoint events; endpoint representations attend to relevant authentication events; cross-attention weights provide natural cross-modal explanation. (2) Cross-modal explanation for threat detection -- Lateral movement detection scenario: input consists of network logs (internal east-west connections), endpoint logs (process execution, registry changes), and authentication logs (successful logins with new credentials). Detection: the system classifies this as high-confidence lateral movement. Cross-modal explanation: network evidence (3 new east-west connections from source host A to hosts B, C, D -- high saliency); endpoint evidence on host A (PsExec service installation, cmd.exe spawned by network service -- high SHAP values); authentication evidence (new login to host B with domain admin credentials 3 minutes after PsExec installation -- high cross-attention weight). Cross-modal narrative: the explanation synthesizes across modalities: PsExec installation on host A (endpoint) correlates with new connections to hosts B, C, D (network) immediately followed by privileged authentication to those hosts (identity) -- the temporal correlation across all three modalities provides high-confidence lateral movement evidence (T1021.002). (3) Explanation attribution across modalities -- Per-modality SHAP: compute SHAP values separately within each modality; identify the most important tokens in network logs, endpoint logs, and authentication logs independently. Cross-modal importance: for late fusion architectures, perturb the fused representation (or mask entire modality contributions) to measure the importance of each modality to the final classification; if masking the authentication modality reduces classification confidence from 0.97 to 0.82, authentication contributes 15 percentage points to the decision -- less than masking endpoint data (confidence drops to 0.41) or network data (confidence drops to 0.65). Modality importance ranking: present per-modality importance alongside per-token importance; for the lateral movement example: Modality importance: Endpoint events (58%), Network events (28%), Authentication events (14%); Top indicators: PsExec service creation (endpoint, SHAP 0.61), connections to 3 new hosts (network, SHAP 0.29), privileged auth to new hosts (authentication, SHAP 0.18). (4) Temporal cross-modal explanation -- Security events unfold over time; cross-modal explanations must capture temporal relationships: timeline explanation format: T+0:00 -- cmd.exe spawns PsExec on host A (endpoint, high saliency); T+0:03 -- SMB connections open from host A to hosts B, C, D (network, high saliency); T+0:05 -- SYSTEM-level authentication to hosts B, C, D via NTLM (authentication, high saliency); T+0:07 -- cmd.exe executes on hosts B, C, D (endpoint, high saliency). The temporal explanation shows the kill chain progression across modalities, directly mapping to ATT&CK tactics: Execution (T1059) → Lateral Movement (T1021.002) → Privilege Escalation (T1078). Temporal attention: for sequence models processing time-ordered events, attention weights across the temporal dimension reveal which time steps are most influential; high temporal attention on the authentication events following the network connections confirms the model is detecting the temporal causal chain rather than individual events in isolation. (5) Cross-modal explanation challenges and mitigations -- Modality imbalance: if network logs are far more voluminous than endpoint logs, the combined input may be dominated by network tokens, causing the model to underweight endpoint evidence even when endpoint signals are more discriminative; mitigation: normalize per-modality token counts or use per-modality attention separately before fusion. Explanation complexity: multi-modal explanations with per-modality and cross-modal components are more complex than single-modality explanations; risk of overwhelming analysts with too much information; mitigation: layered disclosure (top-level summary explanation with expandable per-modality and cross-modal detail for analysts who want it). Missing modality handling: in production, some modalities may be unavailable for specific hosts (endpoint agent not installed, network logging gap); the model must handle missing modalities gracefully; explanations should flag when modalities are missing and note that confidence may be reduced due to missing evidence -- preventing analysts from over-trusting classifications that lack complete evidence.

instruction: How can LLM explanation methods be applied to explain AI-generated YARA rules and Sigma detection signatures?
output: Automated generation of YARA rules and Sigma signatures from threat intelligence or malware samples is an emerging LLM capability. For these AI-generated rules to be trusted and deployed, security engineers need explanations of why the rule was generated, what evidence it is based on, and what threats it detects. XAI for AI-generated detection rules: (1) LLM-generated detection rules -- YARA rule generation: given a malware sample analysis or threat report, LLMs can generate YARA rules targeting the malware family; the rule contains: meta section (rule description, threat actor, reference), strings section (byte sequences, string patterns, regular expressions), and condition section (logical combination of string matches, file characteristics, import functions). Sigma rule generation: given incident investigation findings or threat intelligence TTPs, LLMs can generate Sigma rules for SIEM detection; Sigma rules specify: title and description, log source (product, category, service), detection conditions (field-value pairs with logical operators), and falsepositives section. These generated rules require explanation before deployment: what malware family does this YARA rule detect? What evidence from the malware analysis supports each string in the rule? What attack technique does this Sigma rule detect? What historical incidents or threat intelligence informed the rule logic? (2) Evidence-grounded explanation for YARA rule generation -- For a YARA rule generated from a malware analysis report, explain each rule component with its evidence basis: strings section explanation: string_1 = {4D 5A 90 00} (PE header -- standard for Windows executables, not specific to this malware family); string_2 = {6A 00 68 00 00 00 00 FF 15} (VirtualAlloc call signature -- high confidence malicious, consistent with process injection); string_3 = CreateRemoteThread (function name import -- used for process injection, T1055); string_4 = C2_URL_pattern (URL pattern matching observed C2 infrastructure -- high confidence, specific to this campaign). Confidence annotation: annotate each rule element with its specificity (how many legitimate programs match this pattern?) and sensitivity (what proportion of malware samples from this family match?); high specificity + high sensitivity strings are the most valuable rule components; low specificity strings produce false positives. Source attribution: cite the specific malware analysis finding that motivated each string; string_2 motivated by: dynamic analysis sandbox log line 47, showing VirtualAllocEx called before WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread -- process injection sequence; this source attribution enables rule reviewers to trace each component back to its evidence. (3) Explaining Sigma rule logic -- For a Sigma rule detecting credential dumping via Mimikatz: detection explanation: condition: process_name = lsass.exe AND parent_name in (powershell.exe, cmd.exe, wscript.exe) -- Rationale: lsass.exe is the Windows credential store; Mimikatz accesses lsass.exe memory to dump credentials (T1003.001); legitimate access to lsass.exe from command interpreters is highly unusual and indicative of credential dumping. Threshold explanation: timeframe: 10m; aggregation: count() > 3 -- Rationale: a single lsass.exe access may be a legitimate security tool scan; 3 or more within 10 minutes strongly indicates automated credential dumping rather than manual investigation. False positive rationale: EDR products, Windows Defender, and some AV tools legitimately access lsass.exe; these are excluded via the parent process filter; remaining false positive rate after filter is estimated at 2 per 1000 endpoints per day based on testing against historical data. ATT&CK alignment: T1003.001 (OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory), T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell). (4) Quality evaluation for AI-generated rules -- Before deploying AI-generated detection rules, evaluate: false positive rate (test against 30 days of production log data -- count rule firings on known-clean endpoints; target: false positive rate less than 5 per 1000 endpoints per day for high-priority rules); true positive rate (test against known malicious samples or red team exercise data -- target: detect greater than 90% of representative samples); rule uniqueness (check overlap with existing rules in the detection library -- a new rule that fires on the same events as an existing rule adds cost without adding coverage); and explanation quality review (security engineer reviews the explanation for each rule component and validates that the evidence basis is accurate and the rationale is sound). Automated quality pre-screening: before human review, automatically check: YARA rule syntax validity; string specificity against benign sample corpus; Sigma rule parsability and SIEM compatibility; ATT&CK technique ID validity. Rules that fail automated checks are returned to the LLM for revision before human review. (5) Explanation-driven rule improvement -- When AI-generated rules have quality issues, explanation methods identify which components need improvement: over-broad rules (false positive rate too high): XAI identifies which rule components are present in both malicious and benign samples; the components with high false positive overlap are candidates for removal or tightening; the LLM is re-prompted to generate a more specific variant avoiding the identified over-broad components. Under-sensitive rules (miss rate too high): XAI identifies which malware samples are missed; compare SHAP attributions between detected and missed samples to identify features the model relied on that are absent in missed samples; this identifies where the rule needs additional detection branches. Explanation-feedback loop: analyst review comments on AI-generated rule explanations feed a labeled dataset; rules where the explanation was rated high quality and the rule performed well form positive training examples; rules where the explanation was inaccurate or the rule performed poorly form negative training examples; this feedback loop fine-tunes the rule generation model toward explanation-accurate, high-quality rule generation.

instruction: What is the relationship between LLM calibration and explainability, and how does poor calibration manifest in security-critical deployments?
output: Calibration in LLMs refers to the alignment between expressed confidence and actual accuracy -- a well-calibrated model that says it is 90% confident is correct 90% of the time. Calibration and explainability are deeply related: an uncalibrated model that expresses false confidence undermines the analyst's ability to use explanations correctly, even if the explanations are technically faithful. Calibration and explainability in security LLMs: (1) Calibration fundamentals -- Definition: a model is calibrated if P(correct | confidence = p) = p for all confidence levels p; overconfident model: confidence 0.95 but actual accuracy 0.70 -- the model is wrong 30% of the time when it claims 95% confidence; underconfident model: confidence 0.60 but actual accuracy 0.90 -- the model is correct 90% of the time when it only claims 60% confidence. Expected Calibration Error (ECE): partition predictions into bins by confidence level; for each bin, compute |average confidence - average accuracy|; ECE is the weighted average of these differences across bins; ECE = 0.0 is perfect calibration; ECE > 0.10 indicates significant miscalibration requiring correction. For security LLMs: calibration is more important than for many domains because analysts use confidence scores to decide how much human attention to invest; a miscalibrated model causes systematic under- or over-investment of analyst time. (2) How poor calibration manifests in security operations -- Overconfidence manifestation: an overconfident security LLM scores routine alerts at 0.97 confidence when many are false positives (true accuracy 0.75 at that confidence level); analysts who trust the model's confidence score adopt a triage policy based on the expressed confidence; they auto-close many high-confidence alerts without review; a significant fraction of auto-closed alerts are true positives -- incidents are missed because the model's overconfidence caused under-investigation. Underconfidence manifestation: an underconfident model scores obvious threats at 0.60 confidence; analysts see low confidence scores and manually investigate everything; the efficiency gains of AI assistance are lost because the model's underconfidence causes over-investigation of straightforward alerts. Calibration shift post-fine-tuning: fine-tuning often degrades calibration even when it improves classification accuracy; a model that was well-calibrated before fine-tuning may become overconfident after fine-tuning on a security-domain dataset; this is because fine-tuning adjusts the output logits to fit the training distribution, potentially creating overconfidence for the fine-tuning domain while maintaining calibration for other domains. (3) Calibration evaluation for security LLMs -- Reliability diagram construction: sort predictions by confidence into 10 equal-width bins (0.0-0.1, 0.1-0.2, ..., 0.9-1.0); for each bin, compute average confidence (x-axis) and average accuracy (y-axis); plot the resulting points; a perfectly calibrated model falls on the diagonal y=x; points above the diagonal indicate underconfidence (model is more accurate than it claims); points below indicate overconfidence (model claims more accuracy than it achieves). Security-specific calibration: evaluate calibration separately for: alert triage (is the model well-calibrated for the full range of alert types?); threat attribution (is attribution confidence aligned with attribution accuracy?); CVE severity classification (is the severity confidence aligned with actual severity correctness?). Separate calibration for rare events: for rare but high-severity event types (APT indicators, critical infrastructure attacks), evaluate calibration specifically for these rare classes; a model may be well-calibrated overall but poorly calibrated for rare high-severity events that are underrepresented in evaluation data. (4) Calibration correction methods -- Temperature scaling: the most widely used post-hoc calibration correction; add a temperature parameter T to the softmax: softmax(z/T); T > 1 reduces confidence (spreads the distribution, corrects overconfidence); T < 1 increases confidence (sharpens the distribution, corrects underconfidence); calibrate T on a held-out validation set by minimizing negative log-likelihood; apply the calibrated T at inference time; temperature scaling is parameter-efficient (one additional scalar parameter) and does not change model accuracy, only confidence scores. Platt scaling: fit a logistic regression on the model's logit outputs using the validation set; the logistic regression learns to map raw logits to calibrated probabilities; more flexible than temperature scaling (two parameters: slope and intercept) but also more prone to overfitting on small validation sets. Isotonic regression: non-parametric calibration method; fits a monotone non-decreasing function mapping model scores to calibrated probabilities; most flexible but requires a larger validation set and may not generalize well to out-of-distribution inputs. (5) Calibration-explanation interaction -- Confidence annotation in explanations: display calibrated confidence scores alongside explanations; the explanation tells the analyst what evidence supports the classification; the calibrated confidence tells the analyst how much to trust classifications of that type; together they enable appropriate trust calibration. Explanation-conditioned calibration: some security events are more reliably explained than others; measure calibration separately for alerts with high-quality explanations vs. low-quality explanations; if high-quality explanation alerts are better calibrated (higher confidence-accuracy alignment), explanation quality can serve as a within-alert calibration signal; analysts can apply more skepticism to alerts whose explanations are vague or low-quality, even if the confidence score is high. Calibration for Orion-XAI: after each round of fine-tuning, evaluate calibration on a held-out security classification benchmark; apply temperature scaling correction if ECE exceeds 0.08; document the pre- and post-calibration ECE in the model evaluation report; include calibrated confidence scores in all Orion-XAI outputs alongside the hallucination risk score.

instruction: How are LLM explanations used to support red team exercises that test AI-based security system resilience?
output: Red team exercises against AI-based security systems combine traditional adversarial testing with AI-specific attack surfaces. LLM explanation methods play a dual role: helping red teams understand and attack AI detection systems more effectively, and helping defenders understand and fix vulnerabilities identified during red team exercises. XAI in AI security red teaming: (1) Red team uses of explanation methods -- Evasion surface mapping: before crafting evasion attacks, red teamers use explanation methods to map what the AI detection system relies on; run SHAP or LIME on known-malicious samples that the AI correctly classifies; identify the top-5 features that most strongly drive each detection; these high-importance features are the primary evasion targets -- if the red team can modify or mask these features, they can evade the detection; this intelligence-driven approach to evasion is more efficient than blind trial-and-error. Priority evasion: features with high SHAP values AND known real-world obfuscation techniques available are the highest-priority evasion targets; for malware classification: if process injection API call sequences have the highest SHAP values, obfuscating these calls (using direct syscalls to bypass API monitoring, using alternative injection techniques not in training data) is the highest-priority evasion test. Decision boundary probing: use counterfactual generation to probe the AI decision boundary; systematically vary inputs to find the minimal change that flips the classification; this reveals the shape of the decision boundary and identifies brittle classification regions where small input changes cause large confidence changes. (2) Red team attack types informed by explanations -- Feature masking attacks: red teamers modify the specific tokens that SHAP identifies as high-importance in malware detection; for a malware detection system relying heavily on CreateRemoteThread import: substitute with manual NTDLL function resolution (avoiding the import table entry) and direct syscall implementation (bypassing API hook monitoring); test whether the modified sample evades detection -- confirming the masking attack effectiveness. Adversarial prefix injection: for LLM-based security systems processing text inputs (threat reports, email content), inject adversarial prefixes that manipulate the explanation method without changing the apparent content; a prefix that shifts attention patterns can cause the model to attend to benign context rather than malicious content, reducing detection confidence. Explanation poisoning: if the security system's response to an alert depends on the explanation (e.g., high-quality explanation routes to auto-response), craft inputs that produce specific explanations without corresponding threat behavior; this exploits the gap between the explanation and the underlying model computation. (3) Defender uses of explanation methods after red team exercises -- Failure mode analysis: after a red team successfully evades the AI detection system, analyze the failure mode using explanations: what did the AI classify the evasion sample as? What explanation did the AI generate for its (incorrect) classification? Which features did the AI attend to instead of the malicious features that were masked? This explanation-based failure analysis identifies exactly what the red team changed and why the model failed. Targeted retraining: the failed detection samples, with their red-team-generated variants, form a targeted fine-tuning dataset; including these evasion-successful samples in the next fine-tuning round teaches the model to detect the specific evasion techniques the red team employed; SHAP analysis after retraining confirms that the model now relies on more robust features that are harder to evade. Detection rule augmentation: evasion techniques identified by the red team may be better addressed by rule-based detection than LLM retraining; for evasions based on specific syscall patterns, add rule-based detection of those syscall patterns as a complementary layer; the LLM handles the general case, the rule handles the specific evasion variant. (4) AI red team reporting with explanation evidence -- AI red team reports should include: detected evasion surfaces (SHAP analysis showing which features the target AI system primarily relies on for each detection type); evasion attack details (specific changes made to the input, the SHAP feature importance of the changed features, confirmation that the changed features had high importance in the original detection); evasion results (detection confidence before and after each evasion technique, with explanation comparison); and recommended remediations (targeted fine-tuning dataset composition, feature robustness improvements, complementary rule additions). Explanation evidence quality: attaching explanation evidence to red team findings significantly improves the actionability of reports; a finding that says the AI missed the malware sample is less actionable than a finding that says the AI missed the malware sample because its detection relied on the CreateRemoteThread import function (SHAP value 0.61), which we replaced with direct syscall implementation (detection confidence dropped from 0.94 to 0.12). (5) Continuous red team integration with AI explanation monitoring -- Quarterly AI red team exercises: schedule quarterly red team exercises specifically targeting the AI detection systems; use explanation methods in each exercise to identify the current evasion surface; track how the evasion surface evolves across quarters -- features that the model relies on should become harder to evade as the model is fine-tuned on previous red team findings. Evasion surface metrics: track the minimum number of feature changes required for successful evasion across quarters; increasing this number indicates the AI system is becoming more robust over time; decreasing it indicates the model may be regressing or that the red team has found new attack vectors. Bug bounty for AI evasion: consider a responsible disclosure program for AI detection evasion; external security researchers who find reliable evasion techniques are incentivized to report them rather than exploit them; the program must include explanation evidence requirements -- a valid evasion submission must include SHAP analysis showing what features were targeted and confirmation that the evasion works reliably across multiple test samples.

instruction: How do input attribution methods differ when applied to encoder-only vs. decoder-only LLMs in security classification tasks?
output: Encoder-only models (BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa) and decoder-only models (GPT, Llama, Mistral) have different architectures that affect how attribution methods operate and what explanations they produce. Understanding these differences is important for choosing the right explanation method for security classification tasks. Attribution in encoder-only vs. decoder-only security LLMs: (1) Architectural differences affecting attribution -- Encoder-only architecture: bidirectional attention -- each token attends to all other tokens in both directions; CLS token pooling -- classification is typically performed on the [CLS] token representation; attention patterns are symmetric -- the model can attend forward and backward simultaneously; attribution methods have a natural focal point (the [CLS] token representation that drives classification). Decoder-only architecture: causal (autoregressive) attention -- each token can only attend to previous tokens; for classification, either the last token representation or a special classification token is used; attention is one-directional; for generative explanations, the decoder generates explanation tokens sequentially. Implications for attribution: in encoder-only models, attention from [CLS] to all input tokens provides natural attribution scores; in decoder-only models used for classification, attribution must account for the causal attention pattern; for decoder-only models generating natural language explanations, attribution of the explanation tokens to the input tokens reveals what the model attended to when generating each explanation statement. (2) SHAP and LIME for encoder-only security classifiers -- Encoder-only models (fine-tuned BERT/RoBERTa for security classification) are naturally suited to SHAP and LIME: the input-output relationship is clean (input tokens in, classification probabilities out); SHAP KernelExplainer perturbs by masking tokens (replacing with [MASK]); the [MASK] token is a natural baseline for encoder models, as the model was pre-trained with masked token prediction; LIME fits a linear surrogate on token-masking perturbations. BERT attention for security: BertViz and similar tools provide multi-head attention visualization for encoder models; CLS-to-token attention aggregated across layers (attention rollout) gives attribution scores with a clear interpretation: how much did the CLS representation (used for classification) attend to each input token across the full model. Security classification example: a DeBERTa model fine-tuned for phishing email classification; SHAP attribution on the [CLS] token output shows which email content tokens are most influential; LIME provides an independent cross-check; high agreement between SHAP and LIME on the same tokens provides strong evidence of faithfulness. (3) Attribution for decoder-only security LLMs like Orion-XAI -- Decoder-only models used for security QA and explanation generation (Orion-XAI is based on Llama 3.2, a decoder-only model): attribution for generated explanations: for each generated explanation token, compute gradient-based attribution to input tokens; this reveals which input tokens the model attended to when generating each part of the explanation; a generated explanation sentence citing process injection should show high attribution to the process injection-related input tokens. SHAP for decoder-only models: use SHAP DeepExplainer with the logit for the classification token as the target; perturb input tokens and measure the effect on the classification logit; the causal attention mask means perturbations only affect tokens that come after the perturbed position in the sequence -- account for this in SHAP computation. Baseline selection for decoder-only: the [PAD] token or end-of-sequence [EOS] token is the natural baseline for decoder models (masking an input token with PAD simulates its absence); alternative: use the token with the lowest semantic specificity in the vocabulary as a soft baseline. (4) Attention differences between architectures -- Encoder-only attention: all-pairs attention in every layer; early layers tend to capture local syntax; mid layers capture semantic relationships; late layers capture task-relevant features; CLS attention in late layers is the most informative for classification explanation. Decoder-only attention: causal attention means each token only attends to preceding tokens; for long security documents processed by decoder-only models, token attribution from attention is limited to preceding context; the last token (or a specially trained classification token) attends to the full preceding sequence; late-layer attention from the classification token to preceding tokens gives the most relevant attribution signal for decoder-only classification. Practically: for security classification tasks where highest accuracy is needed, encoder-only models with bidirectional attention often outperform decoder-only models of similar size; for security tasks requiring both classification and natural language explanation generation in a single model, decoder-only models are preferred (they can classify and generate explanations in sequence); Orion-XAI uses a decoder-only architecture for this reason. (5) Choosing the right architecture and explanation method for security tasks -- Task requirements determine architecture: pure classification with highest accuracy and interpretability: encoder-only (DeBERTa, RoBERTa-large) with SHAP on CLS token; classification plus natural language explanation: decoder-only (Llama 3.2, Mistral) with gradient attribution for input influence analysis; interactive security assistant with multi-turn reasoning: decoder-only, with chain-of-thought prompting as the primary explainability method. Hybrid approach: for highest-stakes security decisions, use both: encoder-only model for classification with SHAP attribution (faithfulness-optimized); decoder-only model (Orion-XAI) for explanation generation with CoT reasoning (analyst-friendliness optimized); compare the encoder SHAP explanation with the decoder natural language explanation; agreement between the two explanation types provides additional confidence; disagreement flags the alert for careful manual review.

instruction: How can LLMs with explanation capabilities support AI-assisted penetration testing, and what ethical boundaries must be maintained?
output: AI-assisted penetration testing uses LLMs to accelerate reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, exploit suggestion, and report generation. Explanation methods are important in this context to ensure testers understand the AI suggestions and maintain appropriate oversight of testing activities. Explained AI for penetration testing: (1) Penetration testing workflow and LLM integration -- Pre-engagement phase: LLMs assist with scope analysis, threat modeling, and test plan development; explanation value: the LLM can explain why specific attack vectors are prioritized given the target environment (web application with user authentication, SaaS product with API access) and the relevant threat intelligence; explanation makes the triage reasoning transparent so senior testers can validate scope prioritization. Reconnaissance phase: LLMs process OSINT data (LinkedIn profiles, GitHub repositories, public-facing infrastructure) to identify attack surface; explanation value: when the LLM identifies a potentially exploitable credential leak in a public GitHub repository, it should explain the specific file, line, and credential type, along with the reasoning for why this is high priority (the credential appears to be a production database connection string based on the variable name and format). Vulnerability identification: LLMs analyze scan results (Nmap, Nessus, Burp Suite) and suggest prioritized vulnerabilities; explanation value: when the LLM prioritizes CVE-2024-XXXX, it should explain the exploitability (remote, unauthenticated), the attack complexity (low), the impact (RCE), and why this specific CVE affects the identified service version. (2) Explanation requirements for AI exploit suggestions -- When an LLM suggests an exploitation approach, the explanation must include: technical basis (the specific vulnerability being exploited, the CWE category, the CVE reference if applicable); exploitation mechanism (how the exploit works at a technical level -- what vulnerability class enables it, what the payload does); detection risk (which defenses are likely to detect this approach, and why the suggested technique reduces detection risk); preconditions (what conditions must be true for the exploit to succeed -- access level, network path, target version); and evidence basis (what specific scan finding or reconnaissance finding supports the exploit hypothesis). This explanation structure enables the penetration tester to validate that the AI suggestion is grounded in actual reconnaissance findings rather than generic exploit suggestions. (3) How explanations maintain tester oversight -- Avoiding AI automation of exploitation: AI should suggest and explain, not automatically execute; the explanation allows the tester to evaluate the suggestion and make an informed decision about whether to proceed; automated execution without tester review violates responsible testing principles and potentially scope boundaries. Scope boundary validation: explanation-grounded suggestions reference specific findings from the authorized scope; a suggestion to test a system not explicitly in scope should be immediately identifiable from the explanation (the evidence basis would cite a system not in the authorized target list); explanations that cannot be traced to in-scope findings should be flagged for human tester review before proceeding. Novel technique detection: when the LLM suggests a technique that the tester does not recognize, the explanation provides the basis for validation; a tester who does not understand an AI suggestion should verify the explanation against independent sources before executing; this prevents tester deskilling (over-reliance on AI suggestions without understanding). (4) Ethical boundaries for AI-assisted penetration testing -- Strict scope enforcement: AI penetration testing tools must have hard-coded scope enforcement; the LLM system prompt must specify in-scope targets and should refuse to provide exploitation guidance for out-of-scope targets; explanations that reference out-of-scope targets should trigger automatic rejection and human review. No real malware generation: AI-assisted penetration testing tools should not generate functional malware code even for testing purposes; suggesting exploitation techniques, providing proof-of-concept guidance, and explaining vulnerability exploitation mechanisms within scope is appropriate; generating production-ready weaponized exploits crosses an ethical boundary; this boundary holds even when requested by an authorized tester. Data handling: AI-assisted tools may process sensitive reconnaissance data (employee names, internal IP ranges, credential patterns); data handling must comply with the scope of authorization and applicable privacy laws; LLM processing of sensitive penetration test data must use appropriate data controls. (5) Report generation with explanation support -- AI-assisted penetration test reporting: LLMs can draft vulnerability reports from structured notes; explanation methods ensure reports accurately represent what was found and how. For each finding in the report: finding description (AI-generated description grounded in the specific test output -- no hallucination of unexploited vulnerabilities); evidence section (specific tool output, screenshot references, request/response pairs that evidence the finding); explanation of risk (why this finding matters -- business impact, data exposure, regulatory implications); and remediation guidance (specific, actionable remediation steps grounded in the technology stack identified during reconnaissance). Explanation review: the AI-generated report explanation should be reviewed by the lead tester; discrepancies between the explanation (what the AI says it found and why it matters) and the tester's recollection of the engagement indicate either a reporting error or an AI hallucination; both require correction before the report is delivered to the client. The explanation-review step ensures AI-assisted reports maintain the accuracy and accountability expected of professional penetration testing deliverables.

instruction: How does LLM fine-tuning for security affect the faithfulness and quality of model-generated explanations, and how should this be evaluated?
output: Fine-tuning changes the model's internal representations, potentially affecting both the quality of security task performance and the faithfulness of explanations. Understanding how fine-tuning affects explanations is essential for responsible deployment of fine-tuned security LLMs like Orion-XAI. Fine-tuning effects on explanation quality: (1) How fine-tuning affects explanation faithfulness -- Pre-training vs. fine-tuning representation shifts: the base model (Llama 3.2 3B Instruct) learns general language representations during pre-training; fine-tuning on the security domain shifts these representations toward security-specific features; explanation methods applied after fine-tuning capture the fine-tuned model's reasoning, which should be more security-relevant than the base model's reasoning. LoRA adapter effects on explanations: LoRA fine-tuning modifies only a small subset of the weight matrices (rank-r decomposition); explanations based on weight-dependent methods (gradient-based attribution, probing classifiers) may attribute importance differently based on which weights the LoRA adapter modified; attention-based explanations are less affected by LoRA since attention patterns emerge from the combined base weights plus adapter updates. Catastrophic forgetting effects on explanation: if fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities, explanations may degrade for inputs outside the fine-tuning domain; monitor explanation quality on general security questions (not just the specific types in the training dataset) to detect forgetting. (2) Evaluating explanation quality changes post-fine-tuning -- Pre/post explanation comparison protocol: select a held-out evaluation set of 200 security classification examples with ground-truth important features (labeled by security experts); run SHAP attribution on both the base model and fine-tuned Orion-XAI; measure: ATT&CK alignment (does SHAP highlight tokens corresponding to the correct ATT&CK technique?); expert feature agreement (do SHAP top-10 tokens match the expert-labeled important tokens?); comprehensiveness (does removing SHAP top-k tokens reduce confidence by more than a threshold?). Expected improvements from fine-tuning: SHAP should highlight more security-specific tokens after fine-tuning (domain-relevant terminology, behavioral patterns, ATT&CK-aligned features); ATT&CK alignment should improve because the model has learned security-specific feature representations. Expected risks from fine-tuning: overfitting to training distribution may reduce explanation quality on out-of-distribution security inputs; domain-specific shortcuts learned during fine-tuning may manifest as SHAP over-reliance on features that are correlated with the training distribution but not causally important. (3) Natural language explanation quality evaluation -- For Orion-XAI which generates natural language explanations: ground-truth explanation comparison: for each evaluation example, collect expert-written explanations; compute semantic similarity between Orion-XAI explanations and expert explanations using BERTScore or similar metric; track how this metric changes pre- and post-fine-tuning. Specificity measurement: count the number of specific security entities (CVE IDs, ATT&CK T-codes, specific malware names, concrete IOCs) per explanation; higher specificity indicates better-grounded explanations; track specificity across fine-tuning rounds. Hallucination rate in explanations: specifically measure hallucination in explanation content (as opposed to classification decisions); an explanation that correctly classifies but cites a non-existent CVE or incorrect threat actor is a hallucination failure mode specific to explanation generation; measure the rate of verifiably false statements in fine-tuned model explanations vs. base model explanations. (4) Fine-tuning data design for explanation quality -- Training example explanation quality directly determines output explanation quality: include diverse explanation formats across fine-tuning examples (brief triage explanations, detailed analysis explanations, uncertainty-expressed explanations); include ATT&CK-grounded explanations consistently so the model learns ATT&CK as a standard explanatory framework; include examples where the explanation includes relevant caveats and uncertainty (reduces model overconfidence in explanations). Example format consistency: maintain strict format consistency for explanations in training data; inconsistent formats (some examples use numbered indicators, some use bullet points, some use prose) produce inconsistent model output formats; consistent structured formats enable reliable parsing and downstream automation. Negative example training: include examples where the model should acknowledge insufficient evidence rather than fabricate an explanation; training on refusal-to-explain examples reduces hallucinated explanations for ambiguous inputs. (5) Post-fine-tuning explanation audit procedure -- Immediately after each fine-tuning run, execute the explanation audit procedure: comprehensiveness test (run comprehensiveness metric on 100 held-out examples; compare to pre-fine-tuning baseline; alert if comprehensiveness drops by more than 10%); ATT&CK alignment test (run explanation ATT&CK alignment on 100 held-out examples; alert if alignment drops); specificity test (measure average specificity score on 100 held-out examples; alert if specificity drops); hallucination rate test (scan 100 held-out explanations for verifiably false statements using automated fact-checking; alert if hallucination rate increases); calibration test (measure ECE on held-out classification set; apply temperature scaling correction if ECE exceeds threshold). Explanation audit report: document all metrics in a version-controlled model card that accompanies each Orion-XAI release; include pre- and post-fine-tuning comparison tables; the audit report serves as evidence of due diligence for AI governance requirements and as a reference for future fine-tuning runs.

instruction: How are token-level and span-level explanations different, and when should each be used in security NLP applications?
output: Explanation granularity -- whether to attribute importance at the individual token level or at larger text spans (words, phrases, sentences, paragraphs) -- significantly affects both the information content and the usability of security LLM explanations. Token-level explanations provide maximum granularity; span-level explanations provide maximum readability.
