Token-level vs. span-level explanations in security NLP: (1) Token-level explanations -- Definition: token-level explanations assign an importance score to each individual token in the input; for security NLP, tokens may be subword units (BPE tokenization), full words, or characters depending on the tokenizer; a SHAP token-level explanation for a malicious PowerShell command might assign: high importance to Enc (from EncodedCommand), odedCom, mand (the remaining subword tokens), IEX (Invoke-Expression), and remote URL components. Token-level granularity advantage: maximum precision -- identifies the exact subword units that drive the classification; useful when the distinction between similar tokens is security-relevant (base64-encoded vs. plaintext, CVE-2021-44228 vs. CVE-2021-44229 -- different vulnerabilities). Token-level disadvantage: cognitive overload for analysts reading lengthy security logs -- a 1000-token log with per-token SHAP scores is difficult to interpret visually; subword tokens may be confusing (IEX displayed as I, ##EX when subword-tokenized). (2) Span-level explanations -- Definition: span-level explanations aggregate token importances over text spans defined by linguistic or semantic boundaries; common span levels: word-level (aggregate subword tokens into word units); phrase-level (aggregate tokens for named entities, URLs, command-line arguments, function call sequences); sentence-level (aggregate tokens within each log line or sentence); and paragraph-level (aggregate tokens within thematic sections of a security report). Aggregation methods: sum of SHAP values across span tokens (total importance of span); mean SHAP value (average importance per token in span); max SHAP value (the most important token in the span serves as representative); L2 norm (captures both positive and negative contributions). Span-level advantage: readability -- a sentence-level SHAP explanation for a threat intelligence report shows which paragraphs drove the TTP extraction, which is immediately understandable to an analyst; actionability -- a phrase-level explanation for malware classification shows which function call sequences are most important, directly informing detection rule authorship. (3) When to use token-level in security -- Forensic analysis: when the exact byte-level or character-level feature matters (detecting specific shellcode patterns, exact URL encoding, specific byte sequences in file headers); payload analysis: when the security-relevant information is carried by specific token values (an encoded character sequence, a specific registry key path, a specific CVE ID); model debugging: when investigating why a specific input was classified incorrectly, token-level attribution provides the maximum information for diagnosing the failure; evasion analysis: when testing which specific tokens can be modified to evade the classifier, token-level SHAP values guide the evasion test to the highest-importance positions. (4) When to use span-level in security -- Alert triage: sentence-level explanations for each log entry in an anomaly alert enable analysts to quickly identify the most important log lines without reading individual token scores; threat intelligence processing: paragraph-level explanations for threat reports show which report sections are most relevant to specific threat categories, enabling faster analyst focus during intelligence review; CTI entity extraction: phrase-level explanations for named entities (threat actor names, malware family names, CVE references) show which mentions have the strongest evidence basis; security report generation: span-level explanations provide the natural building blocks for structured reports (this sentence from the log was important because...). (5) Adaptive granularity for security workflows -- Best practice: adaptive explanation granularity that adjusts to the security task and analyst needs: default display: sentence or phrase-level for readability; drill-down: token-level available on demand for specific spans that the analyst wants to investigate further; ATT&CK-aligned span definition: define spans by ATT&CK-relevant behavioral units (a span = one complete API call with its arguments; a span = one authentication event with all relevant fields); this ATT&CK-aligned span definition produces explanations where each span maps naturally to a specific ATT&CK technique. Implementation: for Orion-XAI explanations, compute SHAP at the word level by default (aggregating subword tokens using sum); provide optional token-level expansion for high-importance words; use sentence-level aggregation for long document explanations (threat reports, incident summaries); sentence-level explanations of 3-5 top sentences provide 90% of the analyst value with 10% of the cognitive load of token-level explanations.

instruction: How is self-explanation capability trained into security LLMs, and what are the limits of self-generated explanations?
output: Self-explanation capability -- the ability of an LLM to explain its own reasoning as part of its standard output -- is trained through fine-tuning on explanation-labeled examples. Unlike post-hoc external explanation methods (SHAP, LIME), self-explanations are generated by the model itself, which has advantages and important limitations. Self-explanation in security LLMs: (1) Training self-explanation capability -- Alpaca-format explanation training: in the xai_cybersec_additions.jsonl dataset and the base xai_cybersec_1000.jsonl dataset, training examples follow the Alpaca format with rich, structured explanations as the output field; the model learns to produce explanations in the style and structure of the training outputs; the quality of self-explanations in the deployed model is directly determined by the quality of explanations in the training data. Instruction format for self-explanation: training examples use instructions that explicitly request explanation as part of the output (analyze this log sequence and explain which specific events indicate anomalous behavior and why); this teaches the model that explanation is expected as a standard output component, not an optional add-on. CoT training for self-explanation: training on chain-of-thought examples teaches the model to reason step-by-step before concluding; the CoT trace is a form of self-explanation that makes intermediate reasoning steps visible; models trained on CoT data produce more structured self-explanations than models trained only on direct answer examples. (2) Structure of trained self-explanations -- Well-trained self-explanations for security tasks should include: evidence identification (citing specific input elements -- log entries, token values, behavioral patterns); reasoning chain (connecting evidence to intermediate conclusions); conclusion with confidence (classification with explicit uncertainty where appropriate); ATT&CK mapping (linking identified behaviors to specific ATT&CK techniques); and recommended action (initial triage or investigation step). Training data quality determines structure fidelity: if training examples consistently include all five components, the model learns to include all five; if some components appear inconsistently, the model learns inconsistent behavior; this emphasizes the importance of training data format standardization for self-explanation quality. Orion-XAI self-explanation training: the 3000-example dataset is designed to produce consistent structured self-explanations; every output in the training data follows a structure that can be adapted to the specific question type (QA explanations, analysis outputs, classification explanations). (3) Advantages of self-generated explanations -- Integration: self-explanations are generated in a single model forward pass, unlike post-hoc methods that require additional computation; for real-time security applications, self-explanation eliminates the explanation latency cost of SHAP or LIME. Natural language quality: self-explanations can be written at any level of complexity, using domain-appropriate language, ATT&CK terminology, and contextual references to the specific input; post-hoc numerical attributions require a translation step to produce analyst-readable text. Adaptive explanation: self-explanations can adapt to the complexity of the input -- a simple, clear-cut alert gets a brief explanation; a complex multi-stage attack gets a detailed explanation; post-hoc methods produce the same format regardless of input complexity. Context integration: self-explanations can incorporate contextual information from earlier in the conversation (analyst questions, previous investigation steps, organizational context) that post-hoc methods cannot; in a multi-turn security investigation, the LLM self-explanation can reference previously established context. (4) Fundamental limits of self-generated explanations -- Post-hoc rationalization: the most serious limitation -- there is evidence that LLM self-explanations may not faithfully represent the model's actual internal computations; the model may generate a plausible-sounding explanation that is not causally connected to how it produced the answer; this is analogous to human confabulation (people explaining their decisions based on post-hoc reasoning that differs from the actual decision process). Detecting rationalization: measure whether removing the evidence cited in the self-explanation changes the model's classification; if the model classifies the input the same way when the cited evidence tokens are masked, the self-explanation may be a rationalization rather than a faithful account; comparing self-explanation token importance with SHAP attribution provides a cross-check. Hallucination in explanations: self-generated explanations can hallucinate specific facts (citing a CVE that does not exist, attributing behavior to a threat actor that does not use that technique); post-hoc methods cannot hallucinate specific facts in the same way because they are grounded in actual model computations. Confidence expression: self-explanations may express inappropriate confidence (stating the attack is definitely X when evidence is ambiguous); training on uncertainty-expressing examples helps but does not eliminate this problem. (5) Combining self-explanation with post-hoc validation -- Best practice for security LLM deployment: generate self-explanation as the primary analyst-facing output; run SHAP attribution asynchronously; compare SHAP top-k tokens with the tokens cited in the self-explanation; display an explanation consistency score (proportion of self-explanation-cited tokens that also appear in the SHAP top-k); high consistency score provides additional confidence in the self-explanation; low consistency score flags potential rationalization for analyst review. Automatic fact-checking: extract specific factual claims from self-explanations (CVE IDs, ATT&CK technique IDs, threat actor names); automatically verify each claim against authoritative sources (NVD API, ATT&CK TAXII server, threat actor database); mark unverifiable claims in the analyst interface; analysts see self-explanations with green checkmarks on verified facts and yellow flags on unverifiable claims, enabling efficient targeted skepticism without requiring full manual verification of every explanation.

instruction: How do privacy constraints affect explainability in security AI systems, particularly when explanation data contains sensitive information?
output: Explanation methods in security AI often operate on highly sensitive data -- employee network activity, internal system logs, confidential threat intelligence, and personally identifiable information embedded in security telemetry. Privacy constraints affect what explanations can be generated, stored, and shared. Privacy-preserving explainability: (1) Privacy tensions in security AI explanation -- Explanation as a privacy risk: SHAP and LIME explanations expose which input features drove a decision; in insider threat detection, the input features that drove a high-risk classification include specific employee actions (which files they accessed, which systems they logged into, which emails they sent); an explanation that says this employee was flagged because they accessed the M&A target company research files at 11pm on a Friday reveals sensitive organizational information (an ongoing M&A transaction) alongside the anomalous behavior. Explanation data retention: for audit and post-incident review, security AI systems should retain explanation audit trails; however, these trails contain sensitive security telemetry; the retention period must balance audit requirements (longer is better for post-incident review) with privacy requirements (shorter limits exposure of sensitive personal data). Differential privacy for explanations: adding calibrated noise to SHAP values before storage or display reduces the precision of explanations while preserving privacy of the specific actions that drove the classification; the noise level must be calibrated to provide meaningful privacy protection without rendering explanations useless. (2) Minimum necessary explanation principle -- Explanation content minimization: explanations should contain the minimum information necessary for the intended decision; for first-tier triage, a brief explanation identifying the anomaly category (unusual data access pattern -- accessed 3000 files in 2 hours, 20x above personal baseline) may be sufficient without naming the specific files accessed; for detailed investigation, the full file-level explanation is available but access-controlled to authorized investigators only. Role-based explanation access: implement role-based access control on explanation detail levels: tier-1 analyst: anomaly category and severity, general behavioral pattern; tier-2 analyst/investigator: specific system events, file access patterns, process executions; forensic investigator: full token-level SHAP attribution, complete event timeline; legal/HR: summary explanation suitable for employment action documentation. Access to full explanations should be logged and reviewed to prevent explanation data from being used for purposes beyond the authorized investigation. (3) Federated explanation generation -- In multi-tenant security environments (MSSPs serving multiple clients, shared SOC infrastructure): federated learning consideration: if multiple organizations share a security LLM, explanation data from one organization's alerts must not be exposed to analysts from another organization; explanation computation must be performed within each organization's security boundary. Local explanation generation: deploy model inference and explanation computation within each organization's security perimeter; SHAP and LIME computation occurs on-premises or in the organization's dedicated cloud environment; only the classification output (not the explanation or the input data) crosses organizational boundaries for aggregate model improvement. Explanation aggregation: aggregate anonymized statistics about explanation patterns (which feature categories are most commonly important, which ATT&CK techniques appear most frequently in explanations) can be shared across organizations without exposing specific alert details; this enables detection pattern sharing without privacy violation. (4) Personal data in security telemetry explanations -- GDPR and privacy law implications: security monitoring necessarily processes personal data (employee behavior, communications metadata); GDPR Article 5 requires data minimization -- process only what is necessary; explanations that include personal data must comply with the legal basis for processing; in EU deployments, legitimate interest (security investigation) typically provides the legal basis. Pseudonymization in explanations: replace employee names and identifiers with pseudonymous IDs in stored explanations; the pseudonym mapping is held separately under strict access control; this allows explanation audit trails to be retained for post-incident review without directly containing personal identifiers; re-identification requires access to the pseudonym mapping, which can be access-controlled independently of the explanation database. Explanation retention limits: for routine (unescalated) alerts, explanations should be retained only as long as needed for operational purposes (typically 90 days); for escalated incidents, retain as long as the incident remains active and for the applicable statute of limitations thereafter; implement automated explanation purging tied to retention schedules. (5) Privacy-preserving explanation techniques -- Aggregated counterfactual explanations: instead of explaining why a specific employee was classified as high-risk (which exposes their specific actions), explain what type of behavior would have reduced the risk score (if the user had accessed fewer unique files and had business justification for the access, the risk score would have been below threshold); counterfactual explanations focus on the general decision criteria rather than the specific personal actions, providing decision transparency with reduced personal data exposure. Model behavior explanations: document the security AI model's decision criteria at the population level (global explanations) and publish these as a model transparency statement; employees can understand what categories of behavior the model monitors and flags without individual explanations exposing their specific actions; this supports transparency and employee awareness of monitoring without creating per-employee privacy risks.

instruction: How does the concept of explanation stability impact security SOC operations, and what methods improve explanation consistency?
output: Explanation stability refers to the consistency of explanations produced for the same or similar inputs. In security SOC operations, explanation instability creates practical problems: analysts who receive different explanations for the same alert type cannot develop reliable mental models of AI behavior, leading to either undertrust or inconsistent triage decisions. Explanation stability in SOC operations: (1) Why explanation stability matters in security -- Mental model formation: security analysts form mental models of AI behavior through repeated exposure to consistent patterns; if the explanation for a PowerShell injection alert changes significantly between occurrences, analysts cannot develop the reliable mental model needed for efficient triage; they must evaluate each explanation from scratch rather than applying learned patterns. Audit trail consistency: when security incidents are reviewed post-hoc, explanation consistency is important for legal and compliance purposes; if different runs of the same explanation method on the same input produce different results, the audit trail lacks the consistency needed for regulatory scrutiny. Analyst trust calibration: inconsistent explanations erode analyst trust in the AI system; if the explanation for an alert of type X says feature A is most important one day and feature B the next day, analysts correctly infer that the explanation method is unreliable, and may discount all explanations even when they are accurate. (2) Sources of explanation instability -- Stochastic explanation methods: LIME uses random sampling to generate perturbations; different random seeds produce different perturbation sets and therefore different linear surrogate models; the resulting feature importance rankings can differ significantly between runs, especially when features have similar importance values. MC Dropout: uncertainty estimation via Monte Carlo Dropout uses stochastic dropout masks; each run produces slightly different model outputs; explanations conditioned on model outputs inherit this stochasticity. Numerical precision: floating point operations in gradient computation may produce small differences across runs due to non-deterministic GPU operations; for deep models, these small differences can accumulate and affect final attribution values. (3) Measuring explanation stability -- Local Lipschitz continuity estimation: for a test input x, generate nearby inputs by adding small perturbations epsilon to each token; measure the change in explanation ranking between x and x + epsilon; the ratio of explanation change to input change estimates the local Lipschitz constant; lower values indicate more stable explanations. Rank correlation stability test: for each test input in the stability evaluation set, run the explanation method N=10 times with different random seeds; compute pairwise Spearman rank correlation between all runs; average rank correlation greater than 0.85 indicates acceptable stability for SOC deployment; below 0.7 indicates instability requiring mitigation. Feature set stability: instead of requiring identical rankings, require that the same top-k features appear across runs (set stability); measure Jaccard similarity between top-k feature sets across runs; a Jaccard similarity greater than 0.8 for the top-10 features indicates sufficient stability for analyst consumption. (4) Methods to improve explanation stability -- LIME stability improvements: increase the number of perturbation samples (from 500 to 2000 or more); more samples reduce the variance in the linear surrogate model fitting; cache and reuse the perturbation samples for the same input to ensure identical results on repeated runs; use kernel herding or quasi-Monte Carlo sampling instead of random sampling to reduce variance. SHAP stability: SHAP KernelExplainer inherits LIME sampling variance; use SHAP DeepExplainer or GradientExplainer (which use gradients rather than random sampling) for deterministic explanations when white-box model access is available; for black-box models, run SHAP multiple times and average the results. Ensemble explanation: run multiple explanation methods (LIME, SHAP, gradient saliency) and take the intersection of their top-k features; the intersection is more stable than any individual method because it requires agreement across methods; display only intersection features to analysts, reducing noise from any single method's instability. (5) SOC workflow adaptations for explanation stability -- Explanation caching: for recurring alert patterns, cache the explanation from the first occurrence; subsequent occurrences of the same pattern receive the cached explanation; cache invalidation when the model is updated ensures explanations reflect the current model; caching eliminates per-occurrence variance and reduces latency. Stability warnings: display a stability indicator alongside explanations; low-stability explanations (measured by running the method twice and comparing) receive a yellow indicator warning analysts that the explanation may vary across runs; analysts apply additional skepticism to low-stability explanations. Stability SLA: define a minimum stability requirement for production-deployed explanation systems (Spearman rank correlation greater than 0.85 across 10 runs for 95% of alerts); explanation methods that fall below this SLA are replaced with more stable alternatives or supplemented with ensemble approaches to meet the stability requirement.

instruction: How are large language models used to automatically generate incident timelines and attack narratives, and what role do explanations play in validating these outputs?
output: LLM-generated incident timelines and attack narratives synthesize diverse evidence sources into coherent security incident accounts. These outputs accelerate incident response by reducing the manual effort required to reconstruct what happened during an attack. Explanation methods are essential for validating that AI-generated narratives accurately represent the underlying evidence. LLM-generated incident narratives: (1) Incident narrative generation with LLMs -- Input sources: SIEM alert data (timestamped alert records with source, destination, event type, severity); EDR telemetry (process trees, file operations, registry changes, network connections); authentication logs (login events, privilege escalations, account modifications); network packet captures (partial, for specific suspicious connections); threat intelligence (IOC matches, threat actor profile, known TTPs). LLM processing: the LLM receives all evidence sources as structured context and generates: a chronological incident timeline (ordered list of key events with timestamps, systems involved, and significance); an attack narrative (prose account of the attack from initial access through current state, using kill chain or MITRE ATT&CK framework); an attribution assessment (evidence for or against specific threat actor attribution, with confidence level); a containment priority assessment (which systems and accounts are highest priority for immediate containment); and evidence gaps (what additional investigation is needed to fully reconstruct the incident). (2) Explanation validation for AI-generated timelines -- Evidence grounding check: each event in the AI-generated timeline should be traceable to a specific piece of evidence in the input; for each timeline entry, the explanation should cite the specific log entry, alert, or telemetry record that supports it; timeline entries without clear evidence basis are potential hallucinations requiring investigation. Automated evidence linking: implement an automated check that extracts the specific log references cited in each timeline entry and verifies those records exist in the input data; a timeline entry claiming authentication from host A to host B at 14:32 should correspond to an actual authentication log entry at that timestamp; entries that cannot be matched to input records are flagged for analyst review. Temporal consistency: verify that the timeline is internally consistent (no effect precedes its cause; the initial access event precedes the lateral movement event; the data exfiltration event follows data access events); temporal inconsistency in an AI-generated timeline indicates either hallucination or an error in the LLM's temporal reasoning. (3) ATT&CK-aligned narrative validation -- ATT&CK mapping verification: the AI-generated narrative typically includes ATT&CK technique references; verify each cited technique against the ATT&CK TAXII API; ensure the cited technique IDs match the described behaviors (a technique cited as T1059.001 should involve PowerShell execution as described in the ATT&CK entry); techniques cited that do not match the described behavior indicate ATT&CK hallucination. Kill chain progression logic: the AI-generated narrative should follow a logically coherent attack progression; for a ransomware attack: Initial Access (T1566.001 Spearphishing) should precede Execution (T1059.001 PowerShell) which should precede Persistence (T1547.001 Registry Run Keys) which should precede Discovery (T1083 File and Directory Discovery) which should precede Impact (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact); narrative sequences that violate kill chain logic warrant analyst scrutiny. Coverage assessment: compare the AI-generated narrative's ATT&CK technique coverage against the complete set of detected behaviors in the input evidence; if the input contains evidence of credential dumping (multiple LSASS access events) but the narrative does not mention credential dumping, the LLM has missed a key attack phase; coverage gaps may indicate LLM attention failures on portions of the input. (4) Analyst validation workflow for AI-generated narratives -- Structured validation protocol: after receiving an AI-generated incident narrative, analysts validate using a structured checklist: every timeline event has a specific evidence citation (no hallucinated events); all ATT&CK technique IDs are valid (checked against TAXII); the temporal sequence is logically coherent (no temporal paradoxes); the attribution assessment cites specific TTP evidence rather than generic assumptions; and evidence gaps are documented (not silently glossed over). Explanation audit trail: the explanation for each timeline event (which specific log records support this event) is stored in the incident case management system; this explanation audit trail provides the evidence chain for subsequent legal proceedings, regulatory reporting, or executive briefings. Collaborative editing: analysts should be able to edit AI-generated narratives and flag errors; editing events (which elements were added, modified, or removed by human analysts) serve as implicit labels for model improvement; systematic editing patterns (analysts consistently remove certain types of AI-generated events) identify model failure modes. (5) Confidence-graded narrative presentation -- Confidence tiers for narrative elements: high confidence (confirmed by multiple independent evidence sources, ATT&CK technique matches specific log entries, temporally consistent): presented as confirmed findings; medium confidence (supported by one evidence source, consistent with typical attack patterns but not specifically confirmed, ATT&CK mapping is inferred rather than explicit): presented as likely findings with supporting evidence cited; low confidence (inferred from incomplete evidence, pattern-matching to known attack types without specific confirmation): presented as hypotheses requiring investigation. Analyst interface design: use visual distinction (color coding, confidence badges) to communicate evidence quality alongside narrative content; high-confidence timeline events appear solid; medium-confidence events appear with yellow highlighting and evidence citations; low-confidence hypotheses appear with red highlighting and explicit investigation recommendations; this presentation prevents analysts from treating all AI-generated narrative elements with equal confidence.

instruction: How can concept-based explanations (TCAV, ACE) be adapted for security LLMs to explain decisions in terms of security-relevant concepts rather than individual tokens?
output: Concept-based explanation methods explain model decisions in terms of human-interpretable concepts rather than individual input features. TCAV (Testing with Concept Activation Vectors) and ACE (Automated Concept-based Explanations) are leading concept-based methods that can be adapted for security LLM explanations. Concept-based explanations for security LLMs: (1) Concept-based explanation theory -- TCAV (Kim et al., 2018): learns a Concept Activation Vector (CAV) in the model's internal representation space for each human-defined concept; a CAV is the normal to a linear classifier boundary separating examples with the concept from examples without it; the TCAV score measures how sensitive the model's prediction is to the concept (how much does the output change when the internal representation is shifted in the CAV direction?); positive TCAV score for a concept means the concept increases the model's confidence in the target class. ACE (Ghassemi et al., 2019): automated variant that discovers concepts from the input data without requiring human concept labels; uses image/text clustering to identify groups of similar input segments as automatically discovered concepts; for security, ACE clusters similar log patterns or threat intelligence text segments into concepts without requiring manual concept labeling. Security concept adaptation: rather than explaining in terms of individual tokens (SHAP) or approximate linear models (LIME), TCAV explains in terms of security concepts (process injection, credential dumping, C2 communication, lateral movement, persistence mechanisms). (2) Defining security concepts for TCAV -- Positive concept examples: for each security concept, collect examples from the model's training data or operational data that clearly exhibit the concept; process injection concept: 50 examples of process injection log sequences (VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, CreateRemoteThread sequences); lateral movement concept: 50 examples of lateral movement log sequences (SMB connections to new internal hosts following credential access events); C2 communication concept: 50 examples of command-and-control network patterns (beaconing to external IPs, DNS tunneling, HTTP POST exfiltration). Negative concept examples: randomly sampled normal log sequences or benign network traffic that do not exhibit the concept. CAV training: train a linear classifier on the positive vs. negative examples using the model's layer-N representations as features; the decision boundary normal vector is the CAV for that concept; repeat for each security concept and each layer of interest. (3) Computing and interpreting TCAV scores for security -- TCAV score computation: for a target classification (anomalous activity), compute the directional derivative of the model output with respect to the CAV direction at each test input; average across all test inputs of the target class; a high positive TCAV score for the process injection concept means that increasing the process injection direction in the internal representation increases the anomalous classification confidence -- the model relies on process injection features for its anomaly classifications. Interpretation for SOC: when a security alert is generated, compute TCAV scores for all defined security concepts; present the top-3 concepts with positive TCAV scores as the explanation: this alert was primarily driven by: (1) process injection patterns (TCAV score 0.72), (2) credential access behaviors (TCAV score 0.45), (3) lateral movement indicators (TCAV score 0.31). This concept-level explanation directly maps to ATT&CK tactics and is immediately interpretable by security analysts without requiring token-level expertise. (4) ACE for automatic security concept discovery -- ACE for security LLMs: apply ACE to automatically discover recurring patterns in security telemetry that the model uses for classification; segment security log sequences into overlapping windows; use clustering (K-means or DBSCAN on model layer representations) to group similar windows into potential concepts; for each cluster, compute TCAV-style importance scores; high-importance clusters with consistent semantic content represent automatically discovered security concepts. Discovered concept analysis: human security experts review the automatically discovered concepts to label and validate them; a cluster of log windows containing similar API call sequences may be labeled process hollowing by an expert; concepts that have high TCAV scores but resist human labeling may indicate model reliance on patterns not aligned with established security concepts (a potential shortcut indicator). Dynamic concept discovery: run ACE on rolling windows of production data to discover new security concepts emerging from new attack techniques; concepts that appear in recent data but not in historical data may represent novel TTPs, triggering threat intelligence updates and detection rule development. (5) Limitations and operational integration -- TCAV limitations: concept quality depends on the quality and representativeness of positive examples; if the process injection concept examples are biased toward one specific injection technique (e.g., only classic CreateRemoteThread injection), the CAV may not generalize to novel injection techniques (process doppelganging, phantom DLL hollowing); concept linearity assumption: TCAV assumes concepts are linearly decodable from layer representations; for complex concepts that are nonlinearly encoded (possible for abstract security concepts like attacker intent), TCAV may underestimate the concept's importance. Integration with SOC interface: concept-based explanations are designed for rapid analyst comprehension; integrate TCAV scores into the SOC alert interface as a concept importance panel; display concept names derived from ATT&CK tactics/techniques with proportional importance bars; link each concept to ATT&CK documentation so analysts can quickly access detailed technique information; this concept-level explanation interface complements token-level SHAP details for analysts who want deeper investigation.

instruction: What are the key principles for designing explainable AI systems for cybersecurity that satisfy both technical and regulatory requirements?
output: Designing explainable AI systems for cybersecurity that satisfy both technical requirements (faithfulness, stability, completeness) and regulatory requirements (GDPR, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, sector-specific regulations) requires deliberate architectural choices from the ground up. Explainable security AI design principles: (1) Regulatory landscape for AI explainability in security -- EU AI Act: classifies AI systems by risk level; AI systems used in critical infrastructure security, law enforcement, and critical safety applications may be classified as high-risk; high-risk AI systems must provide documentation of their decision-making logic, undergo conformity assessment, and provide meaningful explanations to affected persons. GDPR Article 22: individuals have the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects; for security AI systems that make consequential decisions (access denial, account suspension, escalation to law enforcement), GDPR requires the ability to provide meaningful explanation to the affected individual. NIST AI RMF: provides a risk management framework for AI systems emphasizing four functions: Govern (establish AI risk management policies), Map (categorize AI risks), Measure (assess risks including explainability), and Manage (treat risks and monitor); NIST AI RMF Measure function includes explainability and interpretability as key risk measurement dimensions. NIS2 Directive (EU): requires appropriate security measures for network and information systems; AI-based security tools used to comply with NIS2 should themselves meet appropriate security and reliability standards, including explainability for audit purposes. (2) Technical design principles for compliant explainability -- Explanation by design (not afterthought): incorporate explainability requirements into the initial system design; selecting model architectures, training data formats, and inference pipelines with explainability in mind from the start produces better explanations at lower cost than retrofitting explanation methods to existing systems. Method pluralism: use multiple explanation methods at different levels (self-explanation, post-hoc attribution, concept-based) to provide multiple perspectives on model decisions; relying on a single explanation method creates a single point of failure if that method produces unfaithful explanations for certain input types. Explanation completeness documentation: document which types of decisions the explanation system covers and which it does not; a system that provides good explanations for alert triage but poor explanations for threat attribution has documented coverage gaps that can be addressed in future development. (3) Governance structures for explainable security AI -- Explanation governance policy: establish a documented policy defining: what types of AI decisions require explanation; minimum explanation quality standards for each decision type; who can access which levels of explanation detail; how explanations are stored and for how long; and how explanation quality is monitored and what triggers model review. Model cards: for each deployed security AI model (each version of Orion-XAI), publish a model card documenting: training data description; evaluation metrics (accuracy, calibration, explanation faithfulness); known limitations (domains where explanations are poor, input types the model handles poorly); explanation method(s) used; and recommendations for appropriate use. AI oversight board: for high-stakes security AI deployments, establish an oversight board (senior security staff, legal, compliance, ethics) with authority to review and approve explanation system design, audit explanation quality, and mandate model updates when explanation quality falls below standards. (4) Explainability testing and certification -- Pre-deployment explainability testing: before deploying a security AI system, execute a structured explainability test plan: faithfulness test (comprehensiveness and sufficiency metrics on held-out test set); stability test (explanation consistency across multiple runs and similar inputs); human utility test (analyst study measuring triage accuracy and efficiency with and without explanations); adversarial explanation test (can an adversary craft inputs that produce misleading explanations?). Ongoing monitoring and certification: establish a continuous monitoring program for explanation quality; define thresholds for re-evaluation or re-certification; document test results in the model governance record; for systems used in regulated contexts (financial services security, healthcare security, critical infrastructure), obtain third-party explanation quality certification. Regression testing: run explanation quality tests after every model update (fine-tuning, hyperparameter change, data update); explanation quality regression (previously passing tests now failing) triggers a review process before the updated model is deployed. (5) User-centered explanation design -- Explanation audience analysis: different stakeholders need different explanation types; tier-1 SOC analyst: brief, actionable explanations in plain language; senior analyst/threat hunter: detailed technical explanations with ATT&CK mapping and evidence citations; CISO/executive: summary explanations focused on business risk and incident scope; compliance officer/auditor: complete documentation of decision logic with source attribution; legal counsel: evidence-grounded explanations meeting evidentiary standards. Explanation accessibility: explanations must be accessible to users without deep AI expertise; use plain language alongside technical detail; avoid jargon beyond the user's professional vocabulary; provide glossaries for AI-specific terms (SHAP value, ATT&CK technique); test explanation comprehensibility with representative users from each audience group before deployment. Continuous improvement from feedback: build analyst explanation feedback into the operational system; feedback on explanation quality (thumbs up/down, specific error flagging) feeds a labeled dataset for continuous explanation quality improvement; track explanation satisfaction by model version and alert type; publish explanation satisfaction metrics alongside detection accuracy in model evaluation reports.

instruction: How does layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) work for transformer models, and how is it applied to explain LLM-based security decisions?
output: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) is a backpropagation-based explanation method that distributes the model output (relevance) backwards through the network layers, assigning attribution to each input feature while conserving the total relevance budget. For transformer models, LRP must account for the attention mechanism and residual connections. LRP for security LLMs: (1) LRP fundamentals and conservation property -- LRP core principle: the relevance score of the output is propagated backwards through the network such that the total relevance is conserved at each layer; for a two-layer network with neurons a and b: R_i = sum_j( (a_i * w_ij / sum_k(a_k * w_kj + epsilon)) * R_j ) where R_j is the relevance of the output neuron j, a_i are input activations, w_ij are weights; the epsilon term prevents division by zero and provides numerical stability. Conservation property: sum of input relevances equals the model output; this completeness property (similar to SHAP) ensures that the explanation accounts for 100% of the prediction without distributing spurious credit or blame. Advantages over gradient methods: LRP avoids the saturation problem (vanishing gradients) by using ratios of activations rather than raw gradients; LRP produces more spatially concentrated explanations (fewer tokens receive non-zero relevance) which are easier to interpret in security contexts. (2) LRP for transformer self-attention -- Attention layer LRP: the attention mechanism computes weighted sum of value vectors: output = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) * V; for LRP backpropagation through attention: relevance flows through both the attention weight path and the value path; standard LRP rules applied to the matrix multiplication operations distribute relevance through both paths; relevance entering the attention output is split between the attention weight computation and the value projection. Residual connection LRP: transformer models use residual connections (output = layer(x) + x); relevance must be split between the main path through the layer and the residual path; equal splitting is the simplest approach; more sophisticated methods use gradient-weighted splitting to assign relevance proportionally to each path's contribution. CLS token relevance: for classification tasks, relevance is initialized at the CLS token output and propagated backwards; the final distribution of relevance across input tokens represents each token's contribution to the classification decision. (3) Applying LRP to security text classification -- Malware report classification with LRP: for a malware family classification report classified as Ransomware with high confidence, LRP produces token-level relevance scores: high positive relevance on encrypt, files, ransom note, C2 communication (ransomware-specific language); near-zero or slightly negative relevance on generic security terms that appear in both ransomware and non-ransomware reports (malware, malicious, attack). LRP vs. attention comparison for security: in a malware classification study: attention weights highlight commonly-attended security terms that appear in both malicious and benign examples; LRP relevance concentrates on ransomware-discriminative tokens; LRP provides sharper, more class-specific explanations than raw attention; this matches the theoretical expectation that LRP, as a gradient-based method with conservation, is more faithful than raw attention. (4) E-LRP and improved LRP variants for security applications -- Standard LRP limitations: the epsilon-LRP rule can produce explanations that are less stable for inputs near the decision boundary; the relevance signs (positive vs. negative) may not be consistently interpretable across all input positions. E-LRP and LRP-alpha-beta: alpha-beta LRP separates positive and negative activation contributions: R_i = alpha * positive_relevance_i - beta * negative_relevance_i (with alpha - beta = 1 and alpha >= 1); alpha-beta LRP with alpha=2, beta=1 is commonly used; for security classification, positive relevance tokens (pushing toward the classified threat category) and negative relevance tokens (pushing against it) are both informative. Transformer-specific LRP (Samek et al., 2021): implements LRP with attention-specific rules accounting for the softmax non-linearity and the scaled dot-product attention; provides more faithful explanations for transformer models than applying standard LRP rules designed for feedforward networks. BERT explanation quality study (Chefer et al., 2021): demonstrates that transformer-specific LRP outperforms both attention-based and gradient-based explanations on faithfulness metrics for BERT classification; this finding extends to security fine-tuned models, suggesting LRP is the preferred explanation method for encoder-only security classifiers. (5) LRP operational integration for security -- LRP computation cost: LRP requires one forward and one backward pass with modified backpropagation rules; computational cost is similar to gradient saliency (much faster than SHAP or LIME); this makes LRP feasible for real-time security alert explanation. Implementation: Captum (PyTorch) provides LRP implementation via LRP class; for transformer models, Ferret library provides transformer-specific LRP implementations; for Hugging Face models, LRP can be integrated by registering custom backward hooks. Security analyst presentation: present LRP results as token highlighting with color coding (high positive relevance in red, high negative relevance in blue, near-zero in gray); for long security logs, present only the top-N most relevant log entries (sorted by their aggregated relevance) rather than the full log with per-token scores; this focuses analyst attention on the most relevant evidence without overwhelming with the full LRP output.

instruction: How are explanation methods used to detect and explain model failures when LLMs encounter out-of-distribution security inputs?
output: Out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs occur when the model encounters inputs that differ significantly from its training distribution. In security, OOD inputs are common and dangerous: novel attack techniques, new malware families, and previously unseen threat actor TTPs are all OOD for a model trained on historical data. Explanation methods are valuable for detecting and characterizing OOD inputs and their associated model failures. OOD detection and explanation in security LLMs: (1) Why OOD is pervasive in security -- Security adversarial dynamics: unlike static domains, security environments change as adversaries adapt their techniques to evade defenses; a model trained on 2023 ransomware TTPs may encounter OOD inputs from 2025 ransomware that uses novel encryption key management, new C2 protocols, or novel persistence mechanisms not in the training data. OOD consequences in security: false negatives (model classifies novel attack as benign because it does not match training patterns); overconfident wrong predictions (model assigns high confidence to an incorrect classification of OOD input); and explanation failure (model produces a generic or incoherent explanation for OOD inputs because it cannot ground the explanation in learned security patterns). The OOD detection problem: unlike errors on in-distribution data (which may be due to model limitations), OOD errors indicate that the model is operating outside its validated reliability envelope; these errors should trigger model update procedures rather than just investigation of the specific alert. (2) Explanation-based OOD indicators -- Explanation coherence as an OOD signal: for in-distribution security inputs, the model produces explanations with specific, recognizable security concepts (concrete ATT&CK techniques, specific malware behaviors, identifiable threat patterns); for OOD inputs, the model may produce: generic explanations (this activity appears suspicious due to anomalous patterns -- without specific pattern identification); contradictory explanations (different parts of the explanation contradict each other -- indicating the model is pattern-matching to conflicting training examples); mismatched explanations (the explanation cites features not actually present in the input -- hallucination is more likely for OOD inputs where the model cannot ground explanation in training patterns). SHAP distribution OOD detection: for in-distribution inputs, SHAP values follow a relatively consistent distribution (certain feature types consistently receive high importance for their threat category); for OOD inputs, SHAP importance may be diffuse (no features receive substantially higher importance than others) or concentrated on unexpected features (syntactic rather than semantic features receiving high importance); track the SHAP value entropy (higher entropy indicates more diffuse attribution, a potential OOD signal). (3) Statistical OOD detection methods -- Maximum softmax probability (MSP): the simplest OOD detector; inputs where the model's maximum class probability is below a threshold (e.g., 0.7) are flagged as potentially OOD; limitation: overconfident models produce high softmax probabilities even for OOD inputs. Mahalanobis distance: compute the Mahalanobis distance of the input's layer representation from the training distribution mean in each class; inputs far from all class means are OOD; for security classification, maintain per-class Gaussian distribution parameters fitted on training data; at inference time, compute Mahalanobis distance for the current input; high distance indicates OOD. Energy-based OOD detection (Liu et al., 2020): compute the energy of the model logits as E(x) = -log(sum_c(exp(f_c(x)))); in-distribution inputs have low energy (confident predictions concentrate probability); OOD inputs have high energy (uncertain predictions distribute probability across classes); energy score is more robust to overconfidence than MSP. (4) Combining OOD detection with explanation for security -- OOD-aware explanation workflow: first apply OOD detection to classify the input as in-distribution or OOD; for in-distribution inputs, apply standard explanation methods (SHAP, LRP) with confidence; for OOD inputs, apply explanation methods with explicit OOD warnings: the explanation may not be reliable because this input type was not represented in the model training data; display SHAP attributions but add: these attributions may reflect surface-level pattern matching rather than deep security understanding due to the novel nature of this input. OOD investigation escalation: OOD inputs flagged by both the statistical OOD detector and the explanation coherence monitor are escalated to senior analysts; the escalation includes: OOD score (how far from the training distribution), explanation coherence score (how coherent the model explanation is), and recommended investigation approach (manual analysis because AI reliability is reduced for this input type). (5) Model update triggers from OOD analysis -- OOD accumulation monitoring: track the volume and types of OOD inputs over time; a sudden increase in OOD alerts for a specific threat category indicates a new attack technique or campaign not covered by the current model; this is an early warning system for gaps in model coverage that should trigger accelerated training data collection for the new technique. OOD-to-training pipeline: OOD inputs that are subsequently confirmed as threats (by analyst investigation or incident confirmation) form the highest-priority training examples for the next fine-tuning cycle; the model failed on these inputs precisely because they were OOD; including them in the next training run directly addresses the OOD failure; track the OOD-to-confirmed-threat pipeline and use it to measure how quickly the model knowledge base keeps pace with the evolving threat landscape.

instruction: How do explanation methods support the validation of LLM-generated MITRE ATT&CK mappings from security telemetry?
output: LLMs can automatically map security telemetry (logs, alerts, behavioral observations) to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, accelerating threat analysis and detection coverage assessment. Explanation methods are essential for validating these mappings and ensuring that ATT&CK labels are based on the correct evidence rather than superficial pattern matching. ATT&CK mapping validation with XAI: (1) ATT&CK mapping with LLMs -- Mapping task: given a log sequence, alert, or behavioral observation, identify the most relevant MITRE ATT&CK techniques (T-codes) and sub-techniques; the mapping should be evidence-grounded -- each identified technique should correspond to specific observable behaviors in the input. Input types for ATT&CK mapping: endpoint telemetry (process executions, file operations, registry modifications, network connections) mapped to Execution, Persistence, Defense Evasion techniques; network telemetry (flow data, packet captures, DNS queries) mapped to Command and Control, Exfiltration, Lateral Movement techniques; authentication logs mapped to Credential Access, Initial Access, Privilege Escalation techniques. Output format: structured ATT&CK mapping with technique IDs, sub-technique IDs, confidence scores, and evidence citations; example: T1059.001 (PowerShell): High confidence. Evidence: powershell.exe spawned by winword.exe, -EncodedCommand argument, base64 payload decoding to IEX Invoke-Expression. (2) Explanation methods for mapping validation -- Evidence-grounded mapping validation: for each ATT&CK technique mapped by the LLM, extract the cited evidence from the mapping output; verify that the cited evidence tokens are present in the input telemetry; if the LLM cites powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand for T1059.001 (PowerShell), confirm that both tokens appear in the input log sequence. SHAP validation of ATT&CK mappings: compute SHAP values for the ATT&CK technique classification; compare the SHAP top-k tokens with the evidence cited in the LLM mapping explanation; high agreement (the same tokens appear in both SHAP top-k and the LLM's cited evidence) provides dual-method validation of the mapping. ATT&CK hallucination detection: the most serious mapping failure is ATT&CK hallucination -- citing a technique that is not supported by the input evidence; for each mapped technique, apply an NLI entailment check: does the input telemetry entail the ATT&CK behavior description? If the entailment score is low, the technique mapping may be hallucinated; flag low-entailment mappings for analyst validation before use in detection rule development. (3) Coverage analysis with explained ATT&CK mappings -- Detection coverage assessment: aggregate ATT&CK technique mappings across all validated incidents and alerts; compute coverage across the ATT&CK matrix (which tactics and techniques appear in mapped incidents); identify coverage gaps (tactics/techniques not appearing in any mapped incidents) that may indicate blind spots in the monitoring infrastructure. Evidence quality for coverage: weight ATT&CK coverage by evidence quality; a technique mapped with high SHAP agreement and verified evidence citation contributes more to coverage confidence than a technique mapped with low SHAP agreement and unverified evidence; the coverage dashboard distinguishes confirmed coverage (high-evidence mappings) from uncertain coverage (low-evidence mappings). Attacker TTP fingerprinting: for each detected incident, the SHAP-validated ATT&CK mapping provides a TTP fingerprint; compare fingerprints across incidents to identify common threat actors (same TTP fingerprint across multiple incidents suggests the same threat actor); explanation validation ensures the fingerprints are based on genuine behavioral evidence rather than superficial text patterns. (4) Systematic ATT&CK mapping evaluation -- Evaluation dataset: collect 300-500 security telemetry examples with ground-truth ATT&CK annotations (created by certified ATT&CK practitioners); for each example, the ground truth includes: correct technique IDs, the specific evidence supporting each mapping, and techniques that should not be mapped (to test false positive rate). Metrics: precision (proportion of mapped techniques that are correct per the ground truth); recall (proportion of ground-truth techniques that are correctly mapped); F1 score; evidence precision (proportion of LLM evidence citations that correctly identify supporting log elements); and ATT&CK hallucination rate (proportion of mapped techniques with no ground-truth support). Baseline comparison: compare Orion-XAI ATT&CK mapping performance against: simple keyword-to-technique rule mapping (baseline); a general-purpose LLM without security fine-tuning (comparison); commercial ATT&CK mapping tools (competitive benchmark); the evaluation report should show the value added by security-specific fine-tuning over both the baseline and the general LLM. (5) Operationalizing validated ATT&CK mappings -- SIEM alert enrichment: automatically tag SIEM alerts with validated ATT&CK technique IDs using the LLM mapping; high-confidence, evidence-validated mappings are applied automatically; low-confidence or evidence-inconsistent mappings are flagged for analyst validation before tagging. Detection rule development from mappings: ATT&CK techniques consistently mapped to specific telemetry patterns inform detection rule development; for a technique mapped with 80% precision to specific log event sequences, write a detection rule targeting those sequences; SHAP-validated evidence patterns provide the specific detection criteria. Threat reporting integration: validated ATT&CK mappings feed threat intelligence reports; each TTP section of the report is backed by SHAP-validated evidence citations; report consumers can trust that ATT&CK technique claims are grounded in verified telemetry evidence rather than analyst interpretation or LLM hallucination.

instruction: How can LLM-generated security explanations be evaluated using human-AI collaboration studies, and what insights do these studies provide for improving explanation design?
output: Human-AI collaboration studies empirically evaluate how explanation systems affect security analyst decision-making, identifying whether explanations improve accuracy, reduce time, and enhance analyst trust calibration. These studies provide actionable insights for improving explanation design that cannot be obtained from purely technical evaluation metrics. Human-AI collaboration studies for security XAI: (1) Study design for security explanation evaluation -- Controlled experiment design: participants are SOC analysts (target population: tier-1 to tier-2 analysts with defined experience requirements); random assignment to conditions: control (alert score only, no explanation), treatment-LIME (alert score plus LIME explanation), treatment-SHAP (alert score plus SHAP explanation), treatment-NL (alert score plus LLM natural language explanation); all participants process the same set of 60 alerts (pre-selected to include true positives and false positives of varying difficulty); measured outcomes: triage accuracy (correct TP/FP classification), decision time (seconds per alert), confidence calibration (correlation between analyst confidence and accuracy), and alert fatigue indicators (accuracy degradation over the session). Ecological validity: the alerts, explanation formats, and interface design should match the target deployment environment as closely as possible; use realistic security telemetry from the organization's own SIEM (anonymized for the study); present explanations in the interface format planned for production deployment; this ensures that study findings generalize to operational performance. (2) Key findings from security explanation studies -- Decision accuracy improvements: studies of XAI in security contexts typically find 10-25% improvement in alert triage accuracy when analysts receive explanation support vs. score-only; natural language explanations tend to show larger accuracy improvements than numerical attributions for analysts without deep ML expertise; the accuracy improvement is largest for difficult ambiguous cases where analyst and AI have complementary knowledge. Time efficiency: explanations typically add 10-30 seconds to alert triage time but reduce the time spent on escalated investigation (because analysts triage more accurately, fewer false positives are escalated to expensive senior analyst investigation); the net time impact depends on the alert volume and the cost ratio between tier-1 triage time and tier-2 investigation time. Trust calibration: without explanations, analyst trust is often poorly calibrated -- analysts either overtrust (accepting all AI recommendations without scrutiny) or undertrust (ignoring AI recommendations entirely); with explanations, analysts develop better-calibrated trust (trusting AI recommendations when the explanation confirms their expert judgment, overriding when the explanation reveals a model blind spot). (3) Explanation design insights from studies -- Insight 1 -- Explanation specificity matters: vague explanations (this activity is anomalous due to unusual patterns) produce worse outcomes than specific explanations (this activity is anomalous because the process spawned a network connection to an external IP -- this process has never made external connections in 30 days of baseline); analysts cannot validate vague explanations against their domain knowledge, so vague explanations do not improve trust calibration. Insight 2 -- ATT&CK framing improves analyst comprehension: explanations framed in ATT&CK terminology (this matches T1059.001 PowerShell execution with T1027 obfuscation) are better understood by analysts familiar with ATT&CK; for analysts not familiar with ATT&CK, plain language descriptions with ATT&CK as supplementary context are more effective; consider ATT&CK familiarity as an analyst characteristic that should influence explanation format selection. Insight 3 -- Negative explanations are valuable: explanations that also describe why an alert might be a false positive (this pattern is also seen in legitimate administrative scripts; check if the source account has administrative duties) improve analyst false positive detection rates; one-sided explanations that only highlight threat indicators are incomplete. Insight 4 -- Explanation fatigue is real: in high-volume alert environments, analysts experience explanation fatigue (decreasing explanation engagement over the session); explanation length and complexity should be minimized for routine alerts; reserve detailed explanations for escalated, high-severity, or ambiguous alerts. (4) Measuring explanation quality from human studies -- Accuracy contribution: measure the marginal improvement in analyst accuracy attributable to each explanation component; this can be done by selectively removing explanation components (ATT&CK mapping, specific evidence citations, confidence calibration, alternative hypothesis) and measuring accuracy impact; the component with the largest accuracy contribution should receive the most prominent visual placement. Explanation-reliance measurement: measure whether analysts are relying on AI explanations in appropriate vs. inappropriate contexts; appropriate reliance: accepting AI-explained recommendations for alert types where AI accuracy is known to be high; inappropriate reliance: accepting AI recommendations for alert types where AI accuracy is known to be low (OOD inputs, novel attack types); track explanation acceptance rate by alert type and compare against known AI accuracy for each type. Analyst workload: measure cognitive load (NASA-TLX scale) during explanation-supported vs. non-explanation-supported triage; if explanations increase cognitive load without improving accuracy, they are poorly designed; well-designed explanations should reduce cognitive load for straightforward alerts while providing value for ambiguous ones. (5) Translating study insights to explanation system improvements -- Iterative design process: run human studies at each major design iteration (not just at final deployment); identify the explanation elements most associated with analyst accuracy improvement; invest design effort in improving these elements in subsequent iterations. A/B testing in production: after initial deployment, run controlled A/B tests in the production SOC environment (some analysts receive updated explanation format, others receive the current format); measure accuracy, time, and trust calibration differences; this real-world A/B testing provides ecological validity that laboratory studies cannot fully capture. Analyst feedback integration: complement controlled studies with continuous analyst feedback collection (explanation quality ratings, free-text improvement suggestions); the combination of controlled study rigor and continuous feedback breadth provides the most actionable input for explanation system improvement across diverse alert types and analyst experience levels.

instruction: What are the key differences between explainability in supervised security classifiers vs. generative LLMs, and how does each require different evaluation approaches?
output: Supervised security classifiers (trained BERT, DeBERTa, or lightweight models on labeled security data) and generative LLMs (Llama, GPT, Orion-XAI) have fundamentally different architectures, output types, and failure modes that require distinct explainability approaches and evaluation methods. Comparing explainability across security ML paradigms: (1) Supervised classifier explainability -- Classifier characteristics: fixed output space (a discrete set of classes: malicious/benign, severity levels, threat category); deterministic output (same input always produces same output, modulo floating point); well-defined ground truth (labeled data enables direct accuracy measurement). Explanation types: input attribution (SHAP, LIME, LRP, Integrated Gradients) assigns importance scores to input tokens relative to a specific output class; the explanation directly answers what features drove the classification to class C; well-defined faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness, sufficiency, AOPC) evaluate explanation quality. Evaluation approach: held-out labeled test set enables direct comparison of predicted vs. ground-truth labels; faithfulness metrics compute the impact of removing high-attribution features on classification probability; human evaluation studies measure analyst accuracy improvement from classification explanations. Security examples: BERT fine-tuned on malware descriptions for malware family classification; DeBERTa fine-tuned on CVE descriptions for severity classification. (2) Generative LLM explainability -- Generative LLM characteristics: open-ended output space (the model generates natural language text of arbitrary length and content); stochastic output (same input with temperature > 0 produces different outputs each run); multi-task capability (the same model can analyze logs, explain concepts, generate reports, answer questions); no single fixed ground truth (multiple correct responses may exist). Explanation types: explaining generative outputs requires both input attribution (what input tokens influenced the generated output?) and output self-explanation (the model's own explanation of its reasoning, embedded in the output); attribution for generative models must specify which output tokens are being explained (the attribution of the first output token differs from the last). Evaluation approach: no single accuracy metric; evaluation requires: factual accuracy (are the specific claims in the generated output correct?); faithfulness of self-explanation (does the explanation accurately reflect the model's reasoning?); output quality (coherence, completeness, security relevance); hallucination rate (proportion of verifiable claims that are incorrect). Security examples: Orion-XAI generating incident summaries, ATT&CK mappings, threat hunting hypotheses, or answering security analyst questions. (3) Explanation method comparison -- Attribution method applicability: SHAP and LIME work well for both classifier and generative LLMs with some adaptation; for classifiers, attribution is relative to a specific class logit; for generative models, attribution can be relative to the probability of each generated token or the probability of a specific classification token. Self-explanation availability: classifiers typically do not generate natural language self-explanations (they output class probabilities, not text); generative LLMs inherently produce text output that can include self-explanations; this makes self-explanation the dominant explanation mode for deployed generative security LLMs. Counterfactual explanations: both classifier and generative models support counterfactual explanations; for classifiers, counterfactuals identify minimal input changes that flip the classification; for generative models, counterfactuals identify minimal input changes that substantially change the generated output (which may or may not change the eventual security conclusion). (4) Evaluation approach differences -- Classifier evaluation: standard metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC) with a labeled test set; explanation evaluation via comprehensiveness and sufficiency on the same labeled test set; inter-annotator agreement for evaluation set labeling quality; concept-level evaluation (do model explanations match expert-labeled important concepts?). Generative LLM evaluation: factual accuracy assessed by automated fact-checking against authoritative sources (NVD, ATT&CK, threat intelligence databases); RAGAS-style evaluation for RAG-augmented generative systems; human evaluation by security experts on dimensions: accuracy, completeness, security relevance, explanation quality; BERTScore or SacreBLEU for surface-level text quality (less important than factual accuracy for security); G-Eval and other reference-free LLM-as-judge evaluation frameworks; hallucination rate specifically measured for security-critical claims. (5) Deployment considerations for each paradigm -- Classifier deployment: lower computational cost; predictable latency; suitable for high-volume, real-time alert triage; limited to the trained task (cannot adapt to new questions without retraining). Generative LLM deployment: higher computational cost; variable latency depending on output length; suitable for complex analysis tasks requiring flexible reasoning; adaptable to new security questions through prompting; higher hallucination risk requiring additional validation. Hybrid deployment (recommended): deploy a supervised classifier for high-volume, real-time alert triage (fast, reliable, explainable with SHAP); deploy Orion-XAI as the analyst assistant for complex analysis, explanation generation, and interactive investigation; the classifier handles scale, the generative model handles depth; the two explanation paradigms complement each other -- SHAP from the classifier provides faithfulness-validated attribution, Orion-XAI provides analyst-readable narrative explanation.

instruction: How are semantic similarity and embedding space analysis used to explain LLM security decisions by revealing representation-level reasoning?
output: Beyond token-level attribution, embedding space analysis reveals how the LLM represents security concepts internally -- which concepts are similar, how representations change through the model, and what decision boundaries look like in representation space. These analyses provide representation-level explanations that complement token-level attribution. Embedding space analysis for security LLMs: (1) Embedding space visualization for security concepts -- t-SNE and UMAP visualization: reduce high-dimensional LLM representations (768 or 4096 dimensions for typical models) to 2D or 3D using t-SNE or UMAP; for a security LLM, visualize representations of: malware family examples (should cluster by family); threat actor TTPs (should cluster by actor if the model has learned actor-specific patterns); ATT&CK technique examples (should cluster by tactic/technique). Security insight from embedding visualization: well-organized embedding space (clear clusters, meaningful distances) indicates the model has learned meaningful security representations; poorly organized embedding space (overlapping clusters, random scatter) indicates the model has not learned the expected security structure and explanations may be unreliable; embedding visualization provides a quick sanity check on model quality before investing in fine-grained attribution analysis. Distance-based similarity explanation: for a query log sequence, find the training examples most similar in embedding space (nearest neighbors); the nearest neighbors serve as example-based explanations (this alert is similar to these confirmed attack examples); the embedding distance translates to an implicit confidence -- small distance to known attacks indicates high confidence, large distance indicates OOD. (2) Semantic similarity for explanation generation -- Sentence embedding similarity: encode the model's generated explanation sentences using a sentence embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or similar); compute cosine similarity between the generated explanation sentences and relevant ATT&CK technique descriptions; high similarity between an explanation sentence and a specific ATT&CK technique description confirms the explanation is semantically aligned with the claimed technique; low similarity with the claimed technique description indicates a potential explanation-ATT&CK mismatch (the explanation language does not match what the ATT&CK technique actually describes). Cross-modal semantic alignment: for multi-modal security inputs (endpoint + network + authentication logs), compute embedding similarity between different modality representations of the same alert; high cross-modal similarity indicates the model is aligning the same threat across modalities (the endpoint injection behavior and the corresponding network C2 activity are being linked); low cross-modal similarity may indicate the model is processing each modality independently without cross-modal integration, which would limit the quality of multi-modal explanations. (3) Representation probing for security reasoning quality -- Security concept linearity: use linear probing to test whether key security concepts are linearly encoded in the LLM representation space; train logistic regression probes for: threat severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low), ATT&CK tactic category, threat actor identity, malware family; high probe accuracy confirms the model has learned linear representations of these security concepts, which are more explainable (linear concepts are captured by linear attribution methods like SHAP) than nonlinear representations. Representation change through fine-tuning: compare embedding space structure before and after Orion-XAI fine-tuning; measure average within-class cosine similarity (should increase after fine-tuning -- examples of the same threat type should cluster more tightly); measure between-class separation (should increase -- different threat types should be farther apart); improved clustering and separation after fine-tuning confirms the fine-tuning has organized the embedding space according to security concepts. Representation drift monitoring: in production, track the distribution of embedding norms and cosine similarity statistics over time; a shift in the embedding distribution indicates the model is encountering inputs whose representations differ from the training distribution (OOD detection via embedding statistics). (4) Explanation through retrieval augmentation -- Retrieval-augmented explanation: rather than generating a new explanation, retrieve the most similar training examples and their explanations from the training dataset; the retrieved examples serve as explanation by example (this alert matches these training examples, which were confirmed instances of process injection with lateral movement); this approach provides explanation grounding that is not susceptible to LLM hallucination since the retrieved explanations are from validated training examples. Dense retrieval for security explanation: use the LLM's own embeddings to perform dense retrieval (encode the query alert using the LLM encoder; retrieve the nearest-neighbor training examples using approximate nearest neighbor search like FAISS); the retrieved training examples are presented alongside the model's generated analysis as corroborating evidence.
